#7833. 16 Types of Blinds Every Homeowner Should Know

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Updated Nov 6, 2026 1:46 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

If you’ve weighed the benefits of curtains, shutters, and blinds in your search for the right window coverings for your home and you’ve settled on blinds, you’re in good company. According to a study by research firm Market Research Future, the size of the window blind market was an estimated $75.48 billion in 2025, and it’s expected to grow to $136.35 billion by 2035. Another research firm, Global Market Insights, found that blinds and shades dominated the window treatment industry in 2025.

With so many different types of blinds on the market, how do you decide which will suit your home best? Whether you’re looking for something sleek and modern or traditional and classic, this guide will help you figure out which ones might be the right pick for your windows.

Blinds are a type of window covering composed of numerous slats, vertical or horizontal, that can be tilted or rotated to adjust the amount of light entering a space. Blinds made of aluminum or vinyl are typically the most cost-efficient types, but there also are blinds crafted of fabric and wood.

They can be installed inside the window frame or above it. Window blinds are typically mounted with specially designed brackets that are sold with the blinds.

The slats are suspended from a track that runs along the top of a window frame. This style of blinds collects less dust than other types of blinds and is easy to clean. The slats just need to be wiped down with a damp cloth.

Best For: Affordability and minimal maintenance

Blinds.com’s vertical blinds are textured, available in a variety of colors, and are guaranteed to fit.

The Home Decorators faux wood Venetian blinds are cordless, making them safe for households with pets or young children.

Mini blinds are like Venetian blinds, with some minor differences. Like Venetian blinds, they are typically made from aluminum or vinyl instead of wood or bamboo. Mini blinds’ slats, however, are usually an inch wide or narrower. While these two types of blinds perform the same way, mini blinds have a sleeker design and thus tend to look more modern and contemporary.

With a minimalist design and cordless operation, the Achim mini blinds are safe and stylish.

Because vinyl blinds are made from PVC and other synthetic materials, they’re a great choice for bathrooms, kitchens, and other areas prone to moisture and humidity. They’re very easy to clean with a cloth or a vacuum attachment. If you’re looking for a window treatment that helps insulate your windows or provides soundproofing, vinyl isn’t your best bet. Still, they are a lot cheaper than wood and other options, if you’re on a budget.

Best For: Budget-conscious shoppers; moisture-prone rooms

Ideal for high-humidity spaces like garages and bathrooms, Bali’s 2-inch vinyl blinds resist chipping and warping and come in dozens of colors.

Wood blinds are a popular choice for those looking to add an element of luxury to their window treatments since wood blinds offer a natural, timeless look that never goes out of style. Not only do they exude sophistication, but they are also incredibly durable and can last for many years with proper care and maintenance. They can be painted or stained to match any color palette, and different slat sizes are available to accommodate shoppers’ specific needs. Wooden blinds tend to be horizontal—or Venetian—style, though vertical wooden blinds are also available.

Best For: Homeowners who are in it for the long haul—these are built to last

Levolor’s 2-inch wood blinds have cordless lift and wand tilt and come in a variety of wood stains.

Sometimes you want the timeless look of a wood blind but don’t have the budget for it. Enter the faux wood blind, which is usually made from PVC or a wood/synthetic blend. Faux wood blinds look like the real deal (though your mileage may vary when it comes to how authentic the wood grain looks), at a fraction of the price. The best part? They can be installed in high-humidity spaces like laundry rooms and bathrooms, where natural wood blinds would mold and warp.

Best for: Budget-conscious homeowners who want a timeless look

Blinds.com’s faux wood blinds are moisture resistant, and available in a variety of wood stains and painted colors.

Aluminum blinds are one of the most popular types of window blinds because of their affordable price and lightweight yet durable design. A sleek, modern look that can complement many decor styles, they are easy to install and incredibly long-lasting. Aluminum blinds also come in a variety of colors, sizes, and textures, allowing homeowners to customize the look of their windows to suit many different aesthetics. In terms of energy efficiency, aluminum blinds help keep a home’s interior cooler by reflecting the sun’s rays away from the window. This helps reduce air conditioning costs since less energy is required to maintain steady temperatures inside the house.

Best For: Easy installation and durability

Sleek and affordable, Blinds.com’s 8-gauge aluminum blinds are available in a variety of neutral colors.

If you’re looking for blinds to cover sliding doors or large windows, consider panel blinds. These window treatments are composed of several panels affixed to a headrail at the top of the window. Each panel is attached to a carrier that slides along a track in order to open or close the blinds. They offer a unique look that differs from standard vertical blinds, making them a great choice for design-forward shoppers.

Roller blinds are technically a type of window shade. An alternative to curtains, these shades are made up of a single piece of fabric material that rolls up and down to control the amount of sunlight that enters the space. Roller shades can be made from a variety of fabrics, ranging from sheer materials to opaque options. While roller blinds might have a reputation for being low quality and not performing well, their design has actually come a long way in recent years.

Chicology’s blackout roller shade has a cordless design and is made from hypoallergenic polyester that won’t attract dust.

UNISHASDES bamboo blinds  partially filter sunlight and come in a variety of sizes and finishes.

Motorized blinds are modern window coverings that you can open and close using a remote control, phone app, or via voice command. Some models have light sensors that automate the opening and closing of your blinds at certain times of the day. Unlike traditional blinds that are adjusted manually, motorized blinds have electric or battery-powered motors that raise and lower them. If you want to be able to control the lighting in a room without ever having to leave your seat, opt for blinds with this feature.

Custom Home Collection’s wood blinds come in over 100 colors and a motorized lift option, which is ideal for smart homes and hard-to-reach windows.

Coolaroo’s knitted HDPE roller shades are mold resistant and block 90 percent of UV rays. Read the review.

Our Recommendation: Coolaroo Exterior Roller Shade at Amazon, priced from $35.25.This exterior window treatment is affordable, cordless, protects against UV rays, and comes in a wide range of finishes.

Sometimes called layered or dual shades, zebra blinds consist of two layers of fabric, each with alternating horizontal bands of sheer and opaque fabric. You can adjust, or roll, the fabric to line up the stripes on the two layers of fabric, meaning opaque is lined up with opaque, and sheer with sheer; this allows light to enter. If you roll the shade such that the opaque stripes on one layer are lined up with the sheer strips on the other layer, the effect is that of an opaque shade, and no light comes through.

Chicology’s zebra blinds are cordless (and thus kid-friendly), light-filtering, and come in three colors.

Also called cellular blinds or cellular shades, honeycomb blinds are constructed of two sheets of fabric that are seamed together horizontally at regular intervals. When looking at these blinds from the side, the resulting pattern somewhat resembles that of a honeycomb. Highly insulating, the design is considered one of the most energy-efficient, and the cellular construction is also good at noise cancellation

Best For: Energy efficiency; homes with a modern vibe

Noise-dampening, cordless, and energy-efficient, the BlindsAvenue honeycomb blinds can be mounted inside or outside the window.

Pleated blinds are made from a single length of woven fabric that is pressed into sharp, horizontal pleats at regular intervals, yielding a zig-zag appearance. The blind is raised or lowered to adjust the amount of light entering the room. While they’re often compared to honeycomb blinds, pleated blinds don’t offer the same insulating properties as cellular blinds. Pleated blinds offer a clean, modern look.

Best For: Decorators in search of an elegant, minimalist look.

Semi-sheer and cordless, these pull-down blinds from Calyx Interiors are available in four colors and several sizes.

Best For: Rooms in which someone needs to sleep during the day.

These cordless, pull-down blackout blinds from Persilux are available in five colors and multiple sizes.

Our Recommendation: Persilux Custom, Cordless Blackout Cellular Blinds at Amazon starting at $63.99. These cordless, pull-down blinds are available in five colors and numerous sizes.

#7831. Yes, Different Curb Colors Have a Meaning — A Guide to Decoding Them

A painted curb can tell drivers where to park, stop, or unload. Here's what red, yellow, green, blue, and white curbs usually mean.

Finding a parking spot isn’t always as simple as pulling up to an empty space. Sometimes different curb colors come with their own parking rules, and drivers might not know what those colors mean. The different curb colors help drivers know where they can park, stop, or drop someone off.

The California Driver’s Handbook lists five common colors: red, white, yellow, green, and blue. But those colors don’t mean exactly the same thing everywhere. Cities have their own parking rules, and some areas have restrictions that only apply during certain hours. Los Angeles, for example, has different rules for loading zones, while Seattle uses yellow paint to mark some areas near driveways that drivers need to keep clear.

Learn what the five colors generally mean and what drivers should know before parking.

Red curbs generally mean drivers can’t stop or park there, even for a few minutes. That includes waiting in the car while someone runs into a store. They’re common near fire hydrants, intersections, and bus stops, where parked cars could block traffic or get in the way. Some red zones still allow buses to stop to pick up or drop off passengers.

White curbs usually allow drivers to stop long enough to pick up or drop off passengers. They’re often found outside hotels, schools, and hospitals.

But they aren’t regular parking spaces. Drivers generally need to stay with their vehicles and leave once their passengers get in or out. Some cities have different rules, though. San Francisco, for example, also allows certain white curbs to be used for quickly loading or unloading goods.

Yellow curbs usually mark loading zones. They’re often found near businesses where delivery drivers need somewhere to stop while dropping off packages or other goods. Commercial vehicles can typically use these areas for a short time, although some cities allow passenger vehicles to stop there, too. These aren’t regular parking spaces, and nearby signs usually explain how long drivers can stop.

Green curbs generally mean drivers can park, but only for a short time. They’re common near businesses where customers might need to stop for a few minutes. The time limit isn’t always the same, so drivers should check the curb or nearby signs before leaving their cars. Some spaces also have parking meters or restrictions during certain hours.

Blue curbs mark parking spaces for people with disabilities. Cities often place these spaces near building entrances to make them easier to access. Drivers need a valid disability parking placard or qualifying license plate to park in these spaces. Without one, they can’t use the spot, even for a quick stop.

The striped areas next to accessible parking spaces also need to stay clear so people have enough room to get in and out of their vehicles.

#7830. How to Polish Wood Furniture

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 6, 2026 4:32 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

If you want to maintain the beautiful, natural look of your wood furniture, take the time to polish it. A good polishing restores the wood’s appearance, bringing out the beauty of the wood grain while helping to conceal minor scratches. Wood polish can also create a protective barrier that repels dust while shielding the finish and wood from spills. Of course, polishing only protects and prolongs the life of your wood furniture if you use the right type of polish and application technique. Use the wrong polish or apply it incorrectly and you can end up with unsightly buildup, streaks, and even permanent damage. We sought expert guidance from Saadet Turlu, founder of Wow by AlpC, a Sheridan, Wyoming-based company that specializes in high-end solid wood furniture.

There are several options when it comes to choosing a polish—or you can make your own furniture polish. Though liquid varieties are easy to apply, wax-based products offer more staying power. And while there are three main types of polish, these categories often overlap as an emulsion can contain oil, silicone, or wax:

Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

While the right polish is key to getting good results when polishing wood furniture, so too is using the right technique.

Remove all objects from the furniture, including lamps, objects and any other decor, so you can apply the polish evenly over the entire piece. You also don’t want these objects to end up with polish residue on them.

Wipe the area down with a dry microfiber cloth or tack cloth to remove any loose dust. Use a Q-tip to clean dust out of crevices around trim and furniture legs. If there is grime or oily fingerprints, use a barely damp cloth to clean thoroughly. If the piece is especially dirty, you may need to conduct a more thorough cleaning before proceeding.

Not all polish is safe for all wood finishes, and you can’t always trust the list of compatible finishes listed on the bottle. Before diving in, test the polish on an inconspicuous spot to make sure it reacts well with the wood finish. An underside area of the furniture or a corner works well.

Never spray wood polish directly onto the wood. Doing so can create streaks or puddling on the furniture surface while also creating overspray that can land on the floor or surrounding furnishings. Instead, apply a small amount of polish to a soft, lint-free microfiber towel. “Apply the polish very sparingly,” Turlu says. “Always wipe in the direction of the wood grain to ensure the product penetrates the pores evenly.” Apply sparingly. Too much polish can leave a sticky film on the wood surface.

Buffing the piece is key to getting an even, attractive finish. Switch to a separate clean dry microfiber cloth and rub the surface of the wood in the direction of the grain using light pressure. “Apply light, consistent pressure and use sweeping motions, following the direction of the wood grain,” Turlu says. “If streaks appear on the surface, it means you are either applying too much pressure or you used an excessive amount of product initially.”

While furniture polish will help to enhance the shine on your furniture and hide minor scratches, it won’t do anything for stains. To remove water stains from wood, start by identifying the type of stain your dealing with:

White water rings: Water rings are often a result of damage to the finish rather than the wood itself. The best way to deal with rings is to use a commercial water marker removes. Make sure the remover is compatible with the type of finish on the wood. If you’re not sure, test the product on a hidden part of the furniture first.

Dark water stains: Dark stains are usually an indication that the stain has reached into the wood fibers. Removing these stains requires a more extensive repair that’s better left to the pros, especially if the furniture is an antique or a family heirloom.

Aim for a polishing schedule of one to three months depending on how heavily the piece of furniture is used. You might polish a dining table or desk once a month, while you may wait three months for less heavily used pieces, like a china cabinet.

Turlu advises specifically against any products containing silicone. “While silicone may provide an immediate, artificial sheen, it penetrates permanently into the wood fibers,” he says. “If that piece of furniture ever needs to be professionally refinished, the silicone will cause the new finish to separate and fail (a nightmare for refinishers).”

A good polishing wax is almost always a better choice than a polishing oil for most furniture. Wax-based polishes create a barrier that not only enhances the look of the wood but also creates a protective barrier against water and scratches that lasts for months. A polishing oil might be easier to apply, but it remains on the surface of the wood and can attract airborne dust.

While this well-known household cleaner is generally safe to use on wood furniture, it is not a polish. It can be used to clean your wood furniture, if it is particularly grimy, before you polish it.

#7829. No Problem with Recognizing Islamic Talaq Divorce from Dubai, When Wife Didn't Want to Stay Married

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Schultz v. Stevenson, decided today by California Court of Appeal Judges Peter Krause, Shama Hakim Mesiwala, and Stacy Boulware Eurie:

In 2004, [the parties] purchased a residential property in Grass Valley, California, taking title as "husband and wife as joint tenants." In 2020, [husband] Schultz obtained a judgment of divorce from [wife] Stevenson in Dubai, United Arab Emirates (UAE). The Dubai divorce decree addressed marital status and child custody only; it made no findings related to division of property or spousal support.

Years later, Schultz commenced an action … to partition the Grass Valley property [by ordering it sold and the proceeds split -EV]. Stevenson opposed partition, arguing that the Dubai divorce decree is not enforceable in California and therefore the property is community property and not subject to partition [since California law does not allow partition of community property among married parties -EV]. The trial court ultimately … [decided] in favor of Schultz, finding that the parties are divorced and that the property is not community property….

Stevenson … argues that the trial court abused its discretion by extending comity to the Dubai divorce decree because it was based on Islamic (Sharia) laws that violate state public policy and constitutional principles of equal protection and due process…. [S]he argues that the Dubai divorce is not entitled to comity because it is based on a talaq pronouncement of divorce, which violates California's public policy favoring gender equality and constitutional protections against gender-based disparate treatment. [Generally, a talaq divorce can only be initiated by a husband. -EV] Stevenson contends therefore that she and Schultz are still married, and that the Nevada County property is community property, which is not subject to partition.

We conclude that Stevenson has failed to show that the trial court erred in extending comity to the Dubai divorce decree.

Under the doctrine of comity, courts of this nation generally will give effect to the judgment of a foreign nation if the foreign court had proper jurisdiction and enforcement of the judgment will not prejudice the rights of United States citizens or violate domestic public policy…. Even if we agree that parts of Sharia law—such as a talaq pronouncement of divorce—are contrary to domestic public policy favoring gender equality and constitutional protections against gender-based disparate treatment, the mere fact that some laws of the foreign nation are inconsistent with those of the sovereign does not preclude application of comity.

The basic principle of judicial comity is that "'a court should not assume to disturb another court's disposition of a controversy unless there are good reasons for doing so.'" The standard for refusing to enforce a foreign judgment on public policy grounds is high and infrequently met. The standard "'is not simply that the law is contrary to our public policy, but that it is so offensive to our public policy as to be "'prejudicial to recognized standards of morality and to the general interests of the citizens….'"' [E]ven when a foreign law offends public policy, 'it may still be applied in a limited context where the potential harm is minimal….'" (See In re Dalip Singh Bir's Estate (Cal. App. 1948) [in context of intestate succession, foreign law permitting polygamy may be applied under principles of comity].)

Here, we are not persuaded that extending comity to the Dubai divorce decree impermissibly prejudiced Stevenson's rights or flouted state public policy favoring gender equality. It is important to remember that the Dubai judgment only adjudicated two issues—marital status and child custody—and that the trial court extended comity to the judgment as it related to the status of marriage only. {Stevenson contends that issues related to child custody and support have been rendered moot as the children have reached the age of majority.} Since Stevenson plainly did not wish to remain married to Schultz, we cannot say that it was an abuse of discretion for the trial court to recognize the Dubai judgment as dissolving marital status.

The premise underlying Stevenson's claim of prejudice appears to be that recognizing the foreign divorce precludes her from obtaining spousal support and an equitable division of the marital property. We disagree with this premise…. As noted, the Dubai judgment only adjudicated the issues of marital status and child custody. It did not address, and therefore has no effect upon, spousal support or the division of community property in California….

In reaching this conclusion, we note that the trial court has ordered the partition and sale of property but has not yet determined how the proceeds will be disbursed, reserving jurisdiction "to order the manner in which the sale proceeds are to be disbursed, and to order equitable adjustments that the Court considers just and appropriate." It is therefore premature for us to consider whether the distribution of proceeds amounts to an abuse of discretion….

Robin D. Shofner (Scale LLP) represents Schultz.

Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. #7828. How To Spot a Flood-Damaged Car Before You Buy It

Learn the subtle signs to look for to avoid buying a flooded car.

With the average cost of a new car approaching $50,000, it can make more financial sense to buy used. But, while the lower price point is appealing, mechanic David Martin says to shop carefully and to check any used car for signs of flooding. “Engine computers, sensors, electrical connectors and wiring are vulnerable to corrosion, expensive to fix and could endanger lives,” he says. Not all cars that have been in a flood will be given a flood title, and unscrupulous sellers will mask this fact from would-be buyers. Ahead, learn how to tell if you’re buying a flood-damaged car, with expert-backed advice from Martin.

Use your nose to detect water damage inside the vehicle. “If the car smells musty or moldy, watch out,” Martin says. “Also, pay attention to cars that have strong air freshener or detergent scents. They could be used to mask flood-related mildew.” Additionally, look for silt or mud in glove compartments or under seats where it may have been overlooked during cleaning. Finding it is a tell-tale sign the car has been flooded. Also look carefully for condensation behind instrument panels and interior and exterior lights.

Check for any rust or flaking metal on the car’s underside, especially on brake lines and around the fuel tank, Martin says. Lift the hood and look for corrosion on the battery terminals and engine components, then open the car doors and inspect the door hinges for signs of rust.

Vehicle upholstery and carpeting can reveal signs of flooding. Feel for dampness and look for stains, as well as loose, wrinkled or buckled carpeting. Additionally, pull seat belts all the way out to check for stains, mildew or mud and look for mismatched or recently replaced carpeting and upholstery.

Turn on the car and do a thorough test of the car’s electrical components. Check the power windows, door locks, seat controls, and backup camera. “Make sure all lights, the air conditioner, heater, wipers, turn signals, stereo and navigation systems work,” Martin says. “And test them more than once.” Even if an electrical component is working, check to make sure it’s working properly. Flickering lights and intermittent functioning can also be signs of water damage.

Flood-damaged cars may be moved across state lines and retitled, so always get a Carfax report, which tracks a vehicle’s complete history regardless of location. Additionally, run the vehicle’s VIN number through the National Insurance Crime Bureau. “The service can identify whether a car has been reported stolen or labeled as salvage by insurance companies due to flooding,” Martin says. “But, while these reports can be helpful, they don’t cover everything.That’s why having a certified mechanic inspect a used car before you buy is a smart investment.”

Even if you don’t suspect a car has been flooded after looking it over yourself, a professional mechanic could catch subtle signs you missed, as well as any other mechanical issues with the vehicle. Ask them to specifically check for signs of flooding.

Yes, a flood-damaged car can still have a clean title and show no record of flooding in its history.

No, not if you intend to drive it. Issues can continue to arise years after a flooding event that can impact the vehicle’s functioning. However, you could buy a flooded car with the intention of using it for parts.

#7826. If You See Cyan Lights on a Car, Here’s What They Mean

Cyan lights could soon appear on more self-driving cars. Here's what the unusual color means and why federal regulators want to standardize it.

Colored lights play an important part in driving safety. Red brake lights mean a vehicle is slowing down, amber turn signals indicate someone is turning, flashing red and blue indicate an emergency, and yellow lights can mean a hazard or warning.

But what about cyan? Drivers might be noticing that color more often in the future as the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recently proposed new federal standards for these lights as automated vehicles become more common.

Learn what the color would mean, where it’s already appearing, and what drivers should expect in the future.

Cyan lights would indicate that a vehicle’s automated driving system is in control and no one inside needs to actively monitor the road. The lights could appear on cars with someone behind the wheel or vehicles that operate without a human driver.

On Oct. 23, NHTSA announced a proposal to establish federal standards for these lights, including their placement and brightness. The lights would remain steady rather than flash, and drivers would be able to see them from all sides of the vehicle. The proposal is part of a broader effort to update safety requirements for automated vehicles, including those NHTSA describes as “vehicles designed never to be driven by a human being.”

“As automotive technology continues to evolve, our safety standards must keep pace with innovation in ways that do not compromise public safety,” NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison said in the agency’s release. “These proposed updates address unnecessary regulatory burdens for vehicles built without traditional manual controls while establishing clear performance standards for automated vehicle marker lamps. By aligning our regulations with today’s technology, we are paving the way for safe innovation and setting clear rules of the road for automated vehicles.”

Cyan would help other drivers, pedestrians, and law enforcement recognize when an automated system is handling the driving. Unlike common driver-assistance features that help with steering or speed, these systems can operate without constant human supervision under certain conditions.

The lights wouldn’t give self-driving cars any special privileges or change how other drivers should behave around them.

Mercedes-Benz has already received permission to use turquoise-colored lights on certain vehicles in California and Nevada. California approved testing on freeways, while Nevada allowed the lights on certain production vehicles.

The lights work with Mercedes-Benz’s Drive Pilot system, which can handle driving under specific conditions. A driver still needs to remain available to take control when requested. The company has tested the lights near the outside mirrors and on the front and rear of its vehicles.

“Mercedes-Benz is committed to standardizing the color turquoise,” the company said in a release, explaining that the goal is to make automated driving systems easier for people to recognize around the world.

Those approvals came before NHTSA’s latest proposal, which could establish a consistent standard for other manufacturers across the country. For now, the new federal rules are still under consideration. Even if NHTSA finalizes them, carmakers wouldn’t have to install cyan lights on self-driving vehicles. Manufacturers that choose to use them would need to follow the new standards.

Under the proposal, the lights could turn on when the automated system is driving without someone monitoring the road. They’d have to turn off when a person is expected to resume that responsibility. Drivers wouldn’t need to do anything differently when they see cyan lights, but they’d have a clearer idea of who’s controlling the vehicle.

#7825. Don't Expect a Lame-Duck Supreme Court Vacancy (But There Are Other Nominations to Consider)

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Both the NYT and Bloomberg reports that Justice Alito still intends to finish out the current Supreme Court term.

There has been rampant speculation that one of the older conservative justices (namely Justice Sam Alito or Justice Clarence Thomas) might choose to retire before the end of the year so that President Trump could name a replacement while there is still a Republican majority in the Senate. But that is all it is: Speculation.

I have previously predicted that neither Justice Alito nor Justice Thomas would retire during this presidential term (let alone this year). I adhere to this view.

Today, the New York Times and Bloomberg each report that Justice Alito has reaffirmed that he is not planning to retire this year, and that this week's election results have not altered his intentions.

Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. has told people close to him that he does not intend to retire immediately from the Supreme Court, despite Democrats' commanding win in Senate contests on Tuesday, which means Republicans will hold the chamber for only a short time longer.

As a result, Republicans may have missed the window for President Trump to name a fourth or even a fifth justice to the Supreme Court in the final two years of his presidency.

Justice Alito shared his plans with friends after the election results were clear this week, according to two people close to the justice who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The 76-year-old Alito, an anchor of the court's conservative wing, has been the subject of speculation that he might abruptly step down to let President Donald Trump fill the vacancy before Republicans relinquish control of the Senate in January. Such a move could extend Trump's imprint on the court by letting him add a younger, conservative jurist to serve for decades.

The chatter has continued even though Alito said in an interview with Bloomberg News in late September that he had decided to remain no matter how the election turned out. "I intend to stick around through this term," he said then, referring to the nine-month court session that runs through June. "I made that decision many months ago."

Alito indicated that stance hasn't changed despite the Democratic takeover in Tuesday's election, said the person, who asked not to be identified discussing a private conversation with the justice on Wednesday.

While there is no equivalent report on Justice Thomas, there is little reason to think he is going anywhere. Justice Thomas is on the verge of becoming the longest serving justice in the nation's history. Moreover, Justice Thomas has previously said he intends to spend at least 43 years on the Court. Were he to stick to that plan, he would have several more years to go.

While there may not be a Supreme Court nomination to keep the Senate busy during the lame-duck period, there are lower court nominations to consider, including nominees for the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the Fifth, Eighth, and Tenth Circuits. As Michael Fragoso notes in the Wall Street Journal, the lame duck may be Republicans' last opportunity to confirm conservative constitutionalist judges for some time.

Republican senators can make a difference and send a message by putting the Constitution first and confirming the originalist nominees now pending. Petty or parochial squabbles with Mr. Trump may get favorable headlines today but they will be forgotten in a week. A judicial appointment can last a lifetime.

#7822. "The Time, the Opportunity, and the Need to Reclaim the Republican Party from Trump and Trumpism"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

I thought I'd pass along this smart and readable analysis from Bill Otis (Ringside at the Reckoning); as I've mentioned before, he and his coauthor Paul Mirengoff are my go-to people for hardheaded, pragmatic, but principled conservative views. They are probably on balance more conservative than I am, but I always much enjoy their legal and political commentary. An excerpt:

In an election where overwhelmingly the preeminent issue was affordability — in other and more candid words, the increasingly obvious decline in the standard of living huge numbers of people are feeling — what has Trump been occupying himself with? Here's a partial list: Building the White House ballroom (from which, in a tone deaf rendition that defies description) he gave his election post-mortem; re-doing the East Potomac Golf Course to make it a "premium" experience; building a Triumphal Arch no one asked for or thought about when they elected him; demanding prosecutions for imaginary vandalism at the Reflecting Pool; invading Greenland; making Canada the 51st state; re-naming Lake Ontario; re-naming the Gulf of Mexico; and perhaps most prominently, making sure his name gets put on the Kennedy Center even though he had nothing to do with its creation. Then there are numerous other items: Trump passports, Trump one-dollar gold coins, and "commemorative" $100 bills, to name three.

Exactly what does this Adventure in Narcissism seem like to the voter — actually, the millions of voters — who feel like they're being stretched thin? You don't need a florid imagination to answer that one. They gave their answer last night.

It's not like Trump has had no successes. He's made three excellent Supreme Court appointments. He has tackled corrosive and unjust racial preferences like no one else had the guts to. He declines to bow to transgender bullying. Objective economic data show that, whatever "feelings" may be, the economy grew at a healthy clip just this last quarter. He used force with Iran when, for nearly 50 years before him, Presidents were content to kick the can down the road as the mullahs got closer and closer to getting the atomic bomb.

These are considerable and important achievements, not less so because Trump often acts like an oaf. But his character flaws throw a wrench into nearly everything he does. It's less that he's an oaf than that he's a child, far too often content to do what's quick and easy while leaving to adults what's messy and hard. The catch is: He's supposed to be the adult. The main thing behind the failures that got Trump his butt-kicking last night is not his classlessness, his carefree attitude [toward] the truth or his gargantuan self-absorption.

The whole thing, as usual, is much worth reading.

#7820. That Hole in Your Ruler Isn’t Random – Here’s What It’s Actually For

That small hole on a ruler has a practical purpose and an unexpected history. Here's why it exists and how people use it.

Almost everyone has used a ruler at some point, whether it was for a school project, measuring something around the house, or drawing a straight line. But even after years of using one, there’s a small detail that’s easy to miss: the hole near the end.

Those holes in rulers aren’t just part of the design. They actually serve a purpose, and the reason they’re there goes back further than most people might expect. Here’s what they’re for, how they were used in the past, and a few other ways they come in handy.

The hole at the end of a ruler is mainly there for storage. It lets people hang the ruler on a hook, nail, or pegboard instead of leaving it in a drawer or on a workbench. This is particularly helpful with longer metal rulers that might not fit in a toolbox.

But the hole has been around for much longer than modern workshops. Years ago, before paper notebooks became common in schools, students practiced writing on small slate boards. They could wipe away their writing with a damp cloth and use the board again.

Some students tied that cloth to their rulers with a piece of string through the hole. That way, they always had something nearby to clean their slates. Schools eventually moved away from slate boards, but the holes remained. Today, they’re mostly there to make rulers easier to hang and store.

Hanging a ruler isn’t the only reason manufacturers add holes. Some rulers have several, and they can serve different purposes depending on where they’re placed. For example, certain school rulers have three holes spaced along one side. These line up with the rings in a standard three-ring binder, so students can keep their rulers with their other school supplies.

Some rulers also have holes that help with drawing circles. A pin through one hole can hold the ruler in place while a pencil in another hole traces a circle as the ruler turns. Not every ruler has holes designed for this, but specialty models like the Creative Grids Quick Trim Ruler do. A compass is still a better choice when exact measurements matter.

Some crafting rulers have holes for more specific jobs. Quilting rulers and templates may have openings that help mark circles or line up fabric before cutting. Others have slots or shaped edges that guide a rotary cutter, making it easier to cut certain shapes.

There are also special rulers for paper crafts and stitching. Some have rows of tiny, evenly spaced holes that help people mark where to make stitches or decorative patterns.

Of course, not every ruler has holes. Smaller plastic rulers often don’t need them, while longer metal versions may have one at each end. It mostly comes down to how the manufacturer expects people to use the ruler. And for everyday measuring, the holes don’t make much difference. A ruler without them can measure just as accurately as one with them.

#7817. Winter Storm Watch vs. Winter Storm Warning: What’s the Difference?

A winter storm watch and winter storm warning mean different things. Here's what each alert signals and how to prepare for dangerous weather.

Tracking severe weather can sometimes feel like it requires a degree in meteorology. With complex scientific terms and technical jargon, it can be difficult to understand what it all means and what should be done to prepare. That’s when the difference between a winter storm watch and a winter storm warning matters.

Both alerts come from the National Weather Service, but they call for different levels of urgency. Here’s how the alerts work and what homeowners should do when they see one.

A winter storm watch means a significant winter storm is possible, but forecasters aren’t yet sure where or when it will hit or how severe it will be. According to the National Weather Service, watches often arrive a day or two before a storm and can cover heavy snow, sleet, or ice.

They give residents time to prepare, even though the storm may not reach their area. As the forecast becomes clearer, the National Weather Service may upgrade the watch to a warning, issue an advisory, or cancel it altogether.

A winter storm warning means dangerous winter weather is expected or already happening. Heavy snow, sleet, or ice could make travel unsafe and cause other problems, including power outages. The amount of snow or ice needed to trigger a warning varies by location.

“Each office knows the local area and will issue Warnings, Watches or Advisories based on local criteria,” according to the National Weather Service. “For example, the amount of snow that triggers a ‘Winter Storm Warning’ in the Northern Plains is typically much higher than the amount needed to trigger a ‘Winter Storm Warning’ in the Southeast.”

Warnings generally arrive closer to a storm’s arrival than watches, although forecasters can issue one before snow or ice begins falling.

A winter weather advisory means snow, sleet, or ice is expected to cause problems, but forecasters don’t anticipate conditions severe enough for a warning. An advisory may signal slick roads or other travel disruptions. While the weather may be less severe than during a warning, residents should still take precautions and monitor local forecasts.

A winter storm watch gives homeowners time to prepare before conditions worsen. That includes checking heating systems, protecting exposed pipes from freezing, and stocking up on food, medications, and other essentials.

“Your primary concerns at home or work during a winter storm are loss of heat, power and telephone service and a shortage of supplies if storm conditions continue for more than a day,” according to the National Weather Service.

Homeowners should have flashlights, spare batteries, and a charged phone in case the power goes out. Checking smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, locating snow shovels, and stocking up on ice melt can also help.

Once a warning takes effect, homeowners should finish their preparations and avoid unnecessary travel. Staying indoors is generally safest during severe winter weather.

If the power goes out, residents can close off unused rooms and wear extra layers to stay warm. Portable generators should always remain outdoors, away from windows and doors. Grills and ovens should never serve as heating sources because they can create serious safety hazards.

Residents should continue monitoring weather alerts throughout the storm. Once conditions improve, homeowners can check for damage and begin clearing snow and ice from walkways and driveways.

National Weather Service, “Winter Weather Warnings, Watches and Advisories” National Weather Service, “Winter Weather Resources and Frequently Asked Questions” National Weather Service, “Prepare! Don’t Let a Winter Storm Take You by Surprise” Federal Emergency Management Agency, “Be Prepared for a Winter Storm”

#7816. Timber Stoves Scout Review: Wood-Fueled Warmth From a Tabletop Heater

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 7, 2026 9:30 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

My family spends a lot of time on our deck, and even when fall evenings start getting chilly, we still find ourselves wanting to be out there. To extend our outdoor living window, we’ve traditionally kept a basket of blankets available by the door and a stack of wood ready by the fire pit. But since building a fire isn’t always convenient, and huddling under a throw isn’t always sufficient, it’s not long before we’re back inside—enjoying our gas fireplace and worrying about the added energy cost only after the bill arrives.

Once we got it set up, Timber Stoves’ Scout tabletop pellet heater provided the perfect solution to our cold-weather woes. After spending many an evening over the last month enjoying eye-level fires that start in just a few seconds, here’s what we love about the unit and what you deserve a warning on before you buy your own.

Bottom line: The Timber Stoves Scout is a stylish, effective solution for outdoor warmth, offering ease of use and maintenance despite initial setup challenges.

Before we started testing the Scout, we definitely had our reservations. In a home with two high-energy dogs and a revolving door of teenagers, was it even safe to have a wood pellet stove on our picnic table? Then there was assembly, which was challenging at first. The instructions weren’t super clear, so we struggled to get the chimney to fit over the main chamber. We ended up using a flat-head screwdriver to nudge open the gap that runs the length of the chimney, and that provided the fraction of an inch it needed to slide on. We also weren’t sure whether to insert the self-tapping screws to keep everything connected (the instructions said yes, but an online video we found implied no—we went with yes). Even getting the pellets to light took a few tries, but once we added a couple of small pieces off some GreenSpark fire starters we had, they took right off.

The good news is that once we got that first fire lit, our worries were a thing of the past. The Scout has an absolutely charming aesthetic, and we quickly fell in love with its functionality as well. The viewing window is perfect for watching your own tiny fire while you share a meal or play a game, and once it’s cranking, it puts out impressive warmth over about a 5-foot radius. We actually got too hot the first night we used it (early evening temps were still in the low 60s), but all we had to do was stop adding pellets from the hopper, and it slowly died down on its own.

Beyond its impressive heat, the Scout tabletop pellet heater features a rugged design that’s clearly built to last. While we weren’t sure it would be safe to have a tall wood pellet stove up off the ground, the weighted base has kept it rock-solid and stable no matter how many times our dogs have crashed into the table. I definitely wouldn’t leave small children unsupervised around an appliance like this, but that’s standard for any fireplace or fire pit.

Upkeep has been a pleasant surprise as well. The dedicated ash collection tray makes cleanup quick and easy—you just dump the cooled ash between uses to keep air flowing freely through the chamber and add fresh pellets to the hopper. After enjoying at least a dozen fires over the past few weeks, the stainless steel body has taken on a pretty purple-and-brown patina in many places, and I’ve simply wiped off any soot that’s collected inside the viewing window with a dry paper towel. All this to say, if I had to assemble it all over again to get to where I am today, I’d do it in a heartbeat.

The holiday season brings warmth, magic, and, often, a welcome touch of festive cheer to our homes, but for those navigating small floor plans or packed closets, the aftermath can quickly turn into a post-holiday headache. Finding room for bulky holiday decorations can quickly take the joy out of this time of year. Fortunately, you can find ways to set the scene in a way that doesn’t require taking up too much of your precious storage space. From collapsible, fold-flat Christmas trees and re-plantable living trees to accents straight from your backyard or the grocery store, there are plenty of clever ways to celebrate big without cluttering your home.

One way to save space after the holiday is to plant your tree in your own backyard. By choosing a living Christmas tree, you’ll save space, reduce waste, and build memories that last for years to come. A living Christmas tree is sold with its roots still attached, often called a “balled and burlapped” tree. Not only will a living tree fill your home with a fresh pine scent, but replanting it provides environmental benefits, such as minimizing waste, reducing deforestation, providing wildlife habitat, and sequestering carbon. You’ll be able to extend your holiday joy by incorporating replanting the tree as part of your celebration with friends and family, and you’ll be able to enjoy it throughout the year. Look for a living Christmas tree at nurseries, garden centers, online retailers like Lynch Creek Farm and Trees.com, and specialized tree farms.

This classic evergreen makes an ideal Christmas tree—and it can be planted in your yard after the holiday.

Minimize how much space you need to store holiday decorations by purchasing some that inflate or pop up. This Pop Up Christmas Tree, for example, is a smart choice. No assembly is necessary, and it comes fully decorated with Christmas balls, ribbons, bows, and lights already in place. The stand collapses and the tree folds flat, so you can easily tuck it away once the holiday ends. You can also look for inflatables like trees, gift boxes, and snowmen that can be used inside or outside. Once deflated, they’ll be easier to store.

Tapping into nature is one of the easiest ways to decorate for the holidays without accumulating endless bins of off-season storage. By foraging organic materials right from your own yard or neighborhood, you can create a naturally elegant scene. Beyond being completely free and eco-friendly, natural décor easily transitions across seasons or can be safely returned to the earth once the festivities end by adding items to a compost bin, shredding branches into garden mulch, using twigs to kindle a fire in your fireplace or fire pit, creating winter backyard shelters for birds, or setting them out for municipal tree recycling.

Food can double as holiday décor, from ornaments to a table runner, without requiring any storage space once your guests have left. Either the decor items will get eaten, or you can place them in a compost bin. Here are some ideas for crafting gorgeous, aromatic pieces using simple grocery store items:

Investing in multipurpose décor is the ultimate strategy for keeping your home festive without adding post-holiday clutter to your storage space. By selecting items that easily transition into everyday accent pieces, you can maintain a warm, welcoming vibe long after the holiday season comes to an end.

#7813. Tool Trials: Putting Ridgid’s Cordless Crown Stapler To the Test

Is a cordless stapler a real upgrade, or just a nice-to-have? I put one to the test to find out.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Last spring, I was sitting at home with my family watching football on a Sunday when my wife caught me doing what I often do: scrolling Zillow. “What don’t you like about the house we’re in?” she asked. I told her that ever since I finished the basement, I’d missed having a shop space to work on projects.

Her answer: “Then build that garage you always wanted.”

Fast forward eight months, and my new garage is up. I’m insulating the main level and sheathing it with OSB before adding cabinets and shelving and moving on to the upstairs. It’s a big garage; we’re talking 30-plus rolls of insulation on the main level, so on a run to pick up the next half-dozen rolls, I wandered down the tool aisle and saw the Ridgid 18V Cordless 3/8-in. Crown Stapler staring back at me.

Beyond getting the garage insulation up faster, it looked like a tool I’d keep using on future wiring and upholstery projects, and the same goes for anyone re-screening a porch, recovering a chair seat, or tacking down low-voltage wire.

A cordless 3/8-in. crown stapler kit with a 2.0 Ah battery and charger, depth adjustment, an onboard wire and screen attachment, and a built-in LED light.

The Ridgid 18V Cordless 3/8-in. Crown Stapler is a 3-lb. battery-powered stapler that runs on Ridgid’s 18V battery platform. It features an integrated LED light, an onboard wire and screen attachment, a depth adjustment knob, and a belt hook.

It drives 3/8-in. crown (T50) staples from 1/4 to 9/16 in. long. Ridgid claims it can drive 105 staples per minute and up to 6,800 staples on a single charge of a 4.0 Ah battery.

One last note, and in full transparency, I’m a regular user of Ridgid tools myself: Ridgid offers a lifetime service agreement on its tools as long as you register them within 90 days of purchase.

My goal was to install a half-dozen rolls of insulation, then run wire to an outlet to try out the wire attachment. I wanted to see how easy the tool was to use, whether it jammed, and what I liked and didn’t like about it.

The short version: this tool is awesome. No jams, nothing wonky. It’s as simple as load, point, and pull the trigger. It took a little playing with the depth knob to get the staples seating at the right depth, but I had it figured out within a handful of staples.

I really like the wire attachment. I try to keep my wiring clean and neat, usually with zip ties and tie mounts. With this attachment, running the wire was simple, and the stapler did it much more neatly than I expected.

I was also pleasantly surprised by the onboard LED light. It has its own trigger, separate from the firing trigger, so I could turn it on only when I needed it.

It’s also easy on the battery. I put up six rolls of insulation during the test and a couple more off camera, and the indicator on the 2.0 Ah battery didn’t budge.

There were a couple of things I didn’t like, though they’re minor. First, Ridgid advertises dry-fire lockout on this stapler, which I took to mean it wouldn’t fire once the staples ran out. On mine, it still did. To be fair, it never marred the work surface, which Ridgid lists as one of the lockout’s benefits, so it may be doing part of its job. But it was annoying to pull the trigger and have nothing come out, and it made it easy to miss that I was out of staples.

I really like this tool. If you’re only insulating a garage, it’s really nice to have, but not essential. You could get by with a standard stapler. That said, the LED light, the wire attachment, and the price, especially with the battery and charger included, make this a tool I know I’ll use more than I expected on future projects.

#7812. Lawprof's First Amendment Case Against Univ. of Kentucky, and a Case's "Journey so Circuitous it Would Make a Baggins Blush"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Judge Benjamin Beaton Tuesday (W.D. Ky.) in Woodcock v. Capilouto (E.D. Ky.):

Ramsi Woodcock, a tenured University of Kentucky law professor, has been under investigation for more than a year for controversial comments regarding Israel and Palestine. The alleged comments varied in both content and forum: an online petition calling for the invasion of Israel, listserv blasts to the University faculty and broader legal academy accusing Israel of genocide, the interjection of far-afield remarks about colonization at an antitrust panel in Hong Kong, shouts of "Free Palestine!" while driving two law students near campus, and more.

None of the remarks came in the classroom and none appears to have disrupted school activities. Yet all related in some manner to his role as a state-employed professor—rendering all the more curious the University's July 2025 decisions to promote him to full professor one week and call him in for questioning (literally) the next. {Curiouser still, Woodcock maintains that the remarks in question dated as far back as February 2024 and were known (at least in part) to the University since March 2024.}

The following week brought a public denunciation from the University's President, the start of a formal investigation into potential harassment under Title VI, reassignment from teaching duties to "professional development," and a (since rescinded) ban from campus. {This first of two "Notice[s] of Investigation" laid out four allegations that Woodcock "may have violated" the University's code of conduct and other policies. The notice declared (without elaboration) that the "investigation … is consistent with the First Amendment" and "addresses requirements under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act." A second notice, based on reports from four students, identified four additional allegations that may have "created a hostile environment on the basis of race, color, or national origin."}

Rather than participate in the investigation, however, Woodcock filed this [federal] lawsuit …. The pleadings characterize his treatment by leaders of the University and its law school as retaliation for protected academic or personal speech, violations of the Due Process and Establishment Clauses, and racial and religious discrimination…. The issue ripe for resolution today is Woodcock's request for temporary emergency relief halting the investigation and reinstating his teaching duties.

This is Woodcock's second or third such request, depending on how one counts. And it follows a journey so circuitous it would make a Baggins blush.

The judge previously assigned to this case held a preliminary-injunction hearing in December 2025. Instead of granting or denying interim equitable relief, however, that judge decided to abstain [under Younger v. Harris] on the ground that the University investigation should precede any federal adjudication. The Sixth Circuit, in the spring and summer of 2026, declined to issue a stay, reversed on appeal, and declined to accelerate the mandate. {See Woodcock v. University of Kentucky (6th Cir. 2026) (Because the "the disciplinary proceedings against Woodcock remain[ed] in a preliminary, investigatory stage," the proceedings were not "ongoing," rendering Younger abstention inapplicable). Concurring with the denial of Woodcock's request to immediately issue the mandate, Judge Gilman wrote that "the panel's opinion" did not "in any way limi[t] the sound discretion of the district court regarding how to proceed on remand," but instead "simply h[eld] that the district court erred in declining to accept jurisdiction based on Younger" without "purport[ing] to dictate what should happen upon remand; i.e., whether the district court should immediately proceed with a ruling on Woodcock's preliminary-injunction motion, or whether it should first consider the University's motion to dismiss, or whether it should stay proceedings to allow for the University to complete its investigation."}

Woodcock, meanwhile, filed a parallel lawsuit and TRO request in state court in September 2026—relief that the Franklin (County) Circuit Judge denied without prejudice. {The Franklin Circuit Court consolidated the new case's request [for] a TRO with the First Amendment suit Woodcock originally filed in federal court seeking to prevent former-Judge Van Tatenhove from assuming his role as dean of the UK Law School. After this Court denied his requests for emergency relief, Woodcock voluntarily dismissed the federal claims and refiled in state court.} The Sixth Circuit then remanded and reassigned this federal case to a judge outside the Eastern District after one of that court's [judges] was appointed dean of the law school. Woodcock had previously filed still another lawsuit—also reassigned here, and also to eventually land in state court—seeking to block the dean's appointment on First Amendment grounds. The University investigation (led by a private law firm) resumed in September. And this Court held a TRO hearing in October. Although the investigator anticipated that this phase of the investigation would finish by November 2, that date has come and gone.

Such unusual litigation can raise unusual—and unusually tricky—legal questions. This is true here, even though the crux of Woodcock's claim is superficially simple: the University leaders (Defendants here) took adverse action (investigation and reassignment) against him because of his constitutionally protected speech (chiefly, at least on his telling, Woodcock's self-titled "Petition for Military Action Against Israel"). But resolving this question, at least in the context of preliminary equitable relief, raises several others that Supreme Court precedent leaves significantly undertheorized.

None of the answers to these questions are obvious based on the record in this Court or the precedential decisions of others. Whether an investigation into speech and related conduct amounts to unconstitutional retaliation depends on whether the First Amendment protected the underlying speech and whether the state's response would deter a person of "ordinary firmness" from speaking similarly. Protection for the speech, in turn, depends on whether Woodcock spoke in either his personal or his "academic" capacity. And even if one of those carve-outs apply, courts may still ask whether the "employee's interest in speaking on a matter of public concern outweigh[s] the employer's interest 'in promoting the efficiency of the public services it performs through its employees.'" {Courts also consider "whether the statement (a) impairs discipline by superiors or harmony among co-workers, (b) has a detrimental impact on close working relationships for which personal loyalty and confidence are necessary, (c) impedes the performance of the speaker's duties or interferes with the regular operation of the enterprise," or (d) undermines the mission of the employer."} Additionally, the appropriateness of interim equitable relief turns on similarly difficult—even incommensurable—considerations, including the burdens on Woodcock's ongoing political speech (which appears to have continued in forums outside the classroom), the Commonwealth's interest in controlling the taxpayer-subsidized education offered to its citizens and future officers of the court, and the public's interest in open dialogue, effective investigations, and the avoidance of harassment.

Each of these determinations, courts have illustrated time and again, is fact-dependent. And although a previous judge held an evidentiary hearing nearly a year ago, time and events have not stood still. Woodcock has not, at least not yet, shown that the mere fact of an investigation would chill an ordinary speaker (to say nothing of a tenured professor) in these strange circumstances from engaging in speech on public questions inside or outside the classroom. After all, a university has an interest in "determin[ing] for itself on academic grounds who may teach, what may be taught, how it shall be taught, and who may be admitted to study."

Nor has Woodcock yet shown that the idiosyncratic lawprof speech at issue—in listservs, foreign conferences, links from the UK website, carpools, and the like—is necessarily protected, heedless of forum or audience. {For instance, whether institutional IT policies that restrict a professor's use of school email resources amounts to a "prior restraint," is hardly clear given the prevalence of content-neutral time/place/manner restrictions. And whether a professor's off-topic panel remarks amount to an unprotected "shout-down" or instead protected academic speech, for example, likewise casts at least some doubt on Woodcock's argument that this amounts to pure academic or political speech.} To be sure, whether he spoke in his professorial capacity is hotly contested by the parties—and cannot be determined with confidence or specificity at this stage.

Whether reassignment from all teaching duties would deter a speaker in a retaliatory manner is a closer question. This is particularly true because the University has seemingly identified no past or future campus disruption, little risk that Woodcock's speech has or will infect classroom instruction, and any reason why responses other than prior restraint would be unavailable if Woodcock stepped outside the bounds of his role in the future. On the other hand, Woodcock hasn't convincingly identified any aspect of this investigation or reassignment that is vindictive, disproportionately burdensome, or otherwise out of the ordinary.

Such showings are neither obvious nor obviously foreclosed on the current record. Indeed, they are not susceptible to prudent resolution by a distant district judge in the middle of a semester, when interim relief measured in two- or four-week increments [the duration of typical TROs -EV] is highly unlikely to benefit Woodcock in a manner that outweighs the concomitant disruption to the University's orderly governance of academic affairs. Since Woodcock bears the burden of justifying temporary emergency relief, but has not carried it, the Court must deny his TRO request. When in doubt, the Sixth Circuit has reminded us, "[t]he administration of the university rests not with the courts, but with the administrators of the institution.

These are important questions worthy of further evidentiary presentation, however. To that end, the Court will schedule a second preliminary-injunction hearing later this month. The balance between state governance and individual speech can tilt too far in either direction, of course, and investigations cannot last forever. In hopes of limiting any federal judicial intervention to its appropriate role, and with "reluctan[ce] to trench on the prerogatives of state and local educational institutions," therefore, the Court sets a preliminary-injunction hearing for Thursday, November 19 ….

UPDATE: I originally stated that the case was from the Western District of Kentucky, and the opinion does indeed have that heading. But, as the text of the opinion explains, the case is being litigated in the Eastern District of Kentucky, though Judge Beaton is a judge of the Western District (who is, for this particular case, sitting by designation in the Eastern District).

#7810. Your Level Might Be the Wrong Size, and It Could Be Throwing Off Your Work

A short level works for some projects, but longer surfaces need a wider check. Learn how to pick the right size and use it accurately.

Levels come in many different shapes and sizes, and figuring out how long a level should be for a certain project isn’t always straightforward. Choosing the right size matters because a level that’s too short can miss uneven spots, while one that’s too long can be difficult to use in tight spaces.

Here’s how much of a surface a level should cover, which sizes work best, and when overhang is okay.

It depends on the project, but a longer level is usually better for checking bigger surfaces. A shorter one might show that the middle of a board is level without catching a problem closer to either end.

The level doesn’t have to stretch across the entire surface, though. A 24-inch level can work on a four-foot shelf, for example, as long as the installer checks several spots along its length. For longer surfaces, a smaller level can sit on a long, straight board to check a wider area. A laser level is another option, especially when lining up things across a room.

The way the level sits on the material matters, too. A little sawdust or dirt underneath can affect the reading, so both surfaces should be clean. The tool also needs to sit firmly without rocking.

There’s no set rule for how much of a surface a level needs to cover, but it should fit comfortably and have enough contact to stay steady.

Different sizes work better for different jobs:

“Use a 4-foot carpenter’s level for framing whenever you have room for its length,” according to The Home Depot. “Warps or waves in the boards can throw off a shorter carpenter’s level.”

Another common concern is whether the level can hang over the edge of whatever is being checked. Some overhang is fine, provided the tool has enough support to stay steady.

If it starts tipping or rocking, a shorter level will likely work better. The bubble doesn’t need to be directly above the material, either. It can still give an accurate reading even when that part of the tool hangs past the edge.

#7809. The Death of Religion?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

A new book challenges the narrative of religious decline in the US

One of the most important developments in American religion over the past several decades has been the rise of the "Nones"—people who tell pollsters they have no religious affiliation. According to the Pew Research Center, about 29% of American adults now fall into this category, compared with 16% in 2007. Among younger Americans, the figure is even higher. Many observers see these numbers as evidence of the continuing secularization of American society.

A provocative new book challenges this conventional wisdom. In The Death of Religion? Nones, Others, and the Flourishing of Faith, sociologist Byron Johnson and historian Thomas Kidd argue that surveys greatly exaggerate the decline of religion in the US. I interviewed Kidd about the book in the most recent Legal Spirits podcast.

The book maintains that conventional surveys, including those conducted by Pew, give a misleading picture of American religious life. People who identify as religiously unaffiliated are not necessarily unbelievers. Some Nones retain religious commitments even though they have no formal connection to a denomination or congregation. Some Americans belong to religious communities that surveys fail to capture adequately, particularly among racial and ethnic minorities. Consequently, surveys may systematically underestimate the vitality of religion in the US.

Of course, there is evidence of genuine decline in some traditional religious institutions, like mainline churches. I asked Kidd about this during our conversation. Still, the authors make a useful point: religious affiliation and religious belief are not the same thing, and trends in one do not necessarily establish equivalent trends in the other.

For me, the most interesting part of the book is its historical account. It turns out that Americans have been worrying about religious disaffiliation for more than two centuries. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, Americans sometimes referred to people without a definite religious affiliation as "Nothingarians" and suggested doing missionary work among them. Orestes Brownson, the famous Transcendentalist-turned-Catholic, maintained that Nothingarians made up the majority of antebellum Americans.

The historical parallels raise an interesting question. Americans have long been suspicious of institutions and hierarchies. It would not be surprising if this suspicion extended to religious institutions as well. Could Americans' longstanding preference for personal autonomy and self-reliance help explain the persistence of religious disaffiliation, even among people who retain spiritual beliefs?

Whether or not one accepts all the authors' conclusions, their book offers an interesting corrective to overly simple narratives about the disappearance of religion in America. You can listen my interview with Kidd here.

#7806. First Circuit Declines to Mandate Religious Exemptions from Public School Vaccination Requirement,

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

at least on an emergency basis while an appeal on the subject is pending.

From We the Patriots USA, Inc. v. Makin, decided Tuesday by First Circuit Judges Gustavo Gelpí and Seth Aframe:

In this case, plaintiffs … move for an injunction pending appeal of a district court's order denying them a temporary restraining order and a preliminary injunction. If we granted the requested injunction, it would bar the defendants from enforcing, against … We The Patriots members who oppose vaccination on free exercise grounds, Maine's vaccination requirements for children enrolling in elementary and secondary schools….

Plaintiffs primarily argue that they are likely to prevail on appeal because the vaccination requirement imposes the kind of substantial burden on parental and religious exercise rights that triggers strict scrutiny, even assuming that the vaccination requirement is generally applicable. They cite Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972) (holding that Wisconsin's law requiring public or private school enrollment until the age of 16 violated Amish parents' Free Exercise rights), and two recent Supreme Court decisions applying Yoder. See Mahmoud v. Taylor (2025) (in a preliminary injunction appeal, "hold[ing] that the [Montgomery County School] Board's introduction of the 'LGBTQ+-inclusive' storybooks — combined with its decision to withhold notice to parents and to forbid opt outs — substantially interferes with the religious development of their children and imposes the kind of burden on religious exercise that Yoder found unacceptable"; "[a] government burdens the religious exercise of parents when it requires them to submit their children to instruction that poses 'a very real threat of undermining' the religious beliefs and practices that the parents wish to instill"); Mirabelli v. Bonta (2026) (per curiam, emergency docket) (vacating Ninth Circuit stay of permanent injunction; California's policies limiting parental notice about their children's in-school, staff-"facilitat[ed]" gender transitioning "likely trigger strict scrutiny under [the free exercise] provision because they substantially interfere with the 'right of parents to guide the religious development of their children' and 'impos[e] the kind of burden on religious exercise that Yoder found unacceptable'").

On the district court record and the papers before us, plaintiffs have not made the necessary heightened showing of a likelihood of success on the merits…. [I]n the posture of seeking an injunction pending appeal, "the bar is harder to clear" because "an injunction does not simply suspend judicial alteration of the status quo but grants judicial intervention that has been withheld by [a] lower court[]" …. It is not obvious that Yoder, Mahmoud, and Mirabelli govern the situation we face given that Maine's vaccination law does not appear to require a student's submission to school-facilitated instruction.

Relatedly, Yoder itself recognized that prior Supreme Court authority allows States to impose the kind of broad public health initiative that underlies this appeal. See Jacobson v. Massachusetts (1905) (holding that law requiring adults to be vaccinated did not "invad[e] any right secured by the Federal Constitution"); Zucht v. King (1922) (holding that law requiring school children to be vaccinated did not violate the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses); Prince v. Massachusetts (1944) (applying the balancing analysis ultimately adopted in Yoder and upholding application of child labor laws over parent's free exercise challenge; citing Jacobson, stating in dictum that a parent "cannot claim freedom from compulsory vaccination for the child more than for himself on religious grounds. The right to practice religion freely does not include liberty to expose the community or the child to communicable disease or the latter to ill health or death"). See Perry v. Marteney (4th Cir. 2026) (cert. petition filed Sep. 4, 2026) (relying on Prince and Jacobson to reverse preliminary injunction in parental free exercise challenge to West Virginia's school vaccination law).

Plaintiffs do not adequately demonstrate that the more recent authority on which they rely clearly shows that the Yoder line of cases applies to a vaccination requirement, especially where the ability of States to impose such a requirement is entrenched in other Supreme Court authority. At this stage of the appeal, plaintiffs have shown only that there is emerging law in this area. But showing the existence of emerging law that may be distinguishable is not enough to warrant the extraordinary relief of an injunction pending appeal….

When a law substantially interferes with parents' religious upbringing of their children and "pose[s] 'a very real threat of undermining' the religious beliefs and practices that the parents wish to instill in their children," then the law must survive strict scrutiny. Mahmoud (quoting Yoder). See Mirabelli (noting that strict scrutiny applies when a school burdens parents' religious upbringing of their children by instituting a policy of not informing parents of students' gender transitions); Mahmoud (stating that a parent's religious upbringing of their children is substantially burdened when a state policy effectively "tell[s] parents that they must abstain from public education in order to raise their children in their religious faiths"). The Supreme Court has rejected narrow readings of its free exercise precedents on parental rights, Mirabelli, which the district court here did by limiting strict scrutiny to instances in which a school directly inculcates values contrary to the parents' beliefs…. Although the State may be able to demonstrate that a compelling interest supports its vaccination requirement, see Prince, Appellees have not made any argument that the requirement survives strict scrutiny. Thus, although I do not predict the ultimate outcome of the strict scrutiny analysis, Appellants have demonstrated a substantial likelihood of success at this stage justifying temporary injunctive relief.

I consider next the harms to the parties, as well as the public interest. There is no dispute that, because of the vaccination requirement, [plaintiff] Childs' son has been deprived of the opportunity to attend public school. Absent a showing that the vaccine requirement survives strict scrutiny, this is a substantial and irreparable harm.

Further, although the State has a legitimate interest in safeguarding the health of its residents, that interest would not be substantially undermined by an injunction pending appeal. Because the State already permits certain students a grace period to vaccinate and because the vaccination requirement does not apply to certain students who previously invoked a religious objection, it does not appear that allowing Childs' son and the children of other WTP members (if any) in Maine to attend school for the short period of this appeal would cause significant harm….

Kimberly Leehaug Patwardhan, Kendall Schutzer, Allan Bradley, Melissa A. Hewey, and Drummond Woodsum represent defendants.
