I wanted to ensure that any window insulation kit we recommended was truly effective and easy to install, so I put each of these kits to the test. I installed each kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions to see how easy they were to install and to determine the components’ quality. I also tested how well the plastic shrank and how easy the wrinkles were to remove. I left them on the windows for 2 days to see how well they worked (I even left a few on permanently to get through the winter). I then removed them to determine what that process was like and how much cleanup there would be.

It’s worth noting that without a laboratory full of expensive machinery and repeatable, consistent conditions, it’s hard to objectively determine which window insulation kits insulated better. However, all the kits we included on this list were effective at stopping any noticeable air movement or condensation.

There are a number of factors to consider when shopping for window insulation kits. They’re available in different foil types, such as plastic, magnetic, and reflective. Features like film thickness, dimensions, reusability, and installation requirements will determine which insulation kit is most suitable for your home.

Several window insulation product types are on the market: plastic film, magnetic barriers, and reflective foil insulation.

Windows come in all sizes, so look for kits with enough film to cover your windows. Most kits come with enough plastic sheets and double-sided tape to seal several windows. It’s essential for shoppers to know their windows’ dimensions to determine which kit will work for their home.

Window insulation kits create a trap for air between the window and the film. That trap is called an air lock. Double-sided tape, which holds the film in place on the window pane, will create an air lock. By pressing the film firmly onto the tape, users can create a strong bond that keeps drafts out.

To create a long-lasting seal, durable film is a must. Durability is often determined by the film’s thickness. Thick film offers more resistance to punctures from kids or pets. It’s also easier to apply correctly, thus establishing a good seal. Thick film does a better job of insulating windows. Standard window film is about 19 micrometers (μm) thick, while heavy-duty film can be as thick as 38 μm.

Some homes have only one or two truly drafty windows, while others have a slew of them. Choose a kit that has enough film to cover all the drafty windows. Many kits come in multipacks that can cover up to 10 windows. They come with sheets of film that can be cut to size, so every window that needs insulation can be covered.

Window insulation kits are meant to be temporary solutions to drafty windows. The good news is that most of these kits are reusable, so buyers won’t have to purchase a new kit every year. Films 19 μm or thicker can be peeled off the double-sided tape, folded up, and stored when winter is over. The double-sided tape won’t be reusable, but a roll of double-sided tape is cheaper than a houseful of window kits.

The best window insulation kits are effective, affordable, and easy to install. Most kits are installed by placing double-sided tape around the perimeter of the window jamb. Then, window film is applied to the tape. At the bottom of the window, the film is attached to a piece of tape on the sill, making a seal. Finally, the film is heated with a handheld blow dryer to create a transparent, airtight seal free from wrinkles.

Still have questions about choosing the best window insulation kits? Here’s some more information to help you decide.

Window insulation kits create an effective barrier preventing cold air from entering a home. Heat-shrink film applied to the window pane with double-sided tape creates an air gap that works like a thermal window.

Insulated curtains do a good job of keeping the cold temperatures at bay, but they don’t create airtight seals to hold back drafts like window insulation kits do. Plus, insulated curtains must be closed to work, so they block natural light. Window insulation film is usually clear, so it doesn’t block those precious rays of winter sun from shining into a home.

Some window insulation kits claim to reduce a home’s energy consumption by up to 35 percent. Users will need to install these products carefully and on every leaky window to maximize their effectiveness.

#7804. I Thought Multi-Tools Were a Gimmick — Then I Took One on a Camping Trip

If, like me, you think multi-tools are gimmicky gadgets, you might change your mind once you discover how handy they are when your toolbox isn’t within reach.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

I admit I scoffed when my partner first started raving about his Leatherman Wave+ multi-tool. I thought it looked like an expensive, over-elaborate gadget that was destined to gather dust in a junk drawer.

However, as a keen hiker and camper, I’ve discovered how useful it is to have pliers, knives, a saw, scissors, files and other tools packed into one compact, quality piece of kit. I’ve also watched my tech-obsessed partner regularly reach for its precision tools when tinkering with his electrical equipment.

Ahead, I’ll share how a tool I once dismissed as a gimmick earned a permanent spot in my pack, and what two experts think makes a Leatherman worth the price tag.

I had to realize that our Leatherman Wave+ isn’t meant to replace a well-stocked toolbox to understand its value. Instead, it fills the gap when dedicated tools aren’t conveniently available or really needed.

At home, I regularly use the tool’s tiny scissors to carefully prune dead leaves from our many houseplants, the knife to open packages and the small screwdriver to tighten the legs on my glasses. My partner is an IT professional who also has an impressive collection of synthesizers, and he regularly reaches for the tool to make small technical repairs and splice wires.

I’ve found the Wave+ even more useful when we’re borrowing my parents’ campervan, hiking, or camping. The bottle opener is handy for those after-adventure beers, the serrated knife slices baguettes for trailside sandwiches, the saw cuts small, dry branches for kindling, and the screwdriver has adjusted our portable stove and tightened folding chairs.

The pocket-sized multi-tool packs 18 functions into a stainless-steel form that measures just four inches when closed and weighs 8.5 ounces. Alongside the tools I’ve mentioned, it has pliers, bit drivers, a wire stripper and crimper, a ruler, an extra knife blade and file, and an admittedly slightly-tricky-to-use can opener.

While I don’t regularly use all 18 tools, and I might never use some, having the selection provides peace of mind, especially in remote places.

Daniel Kilburn, founder of Emergency Action Planning and a preparedness expert, has carried his Leatherman Surge since his military service in 2006. “It’s an expedient tool to have on hand when you know you’re going to be someplace where you won’t have access to any others,” he says.

Scott Emanuel of knives, multi-tools, and outdoor equipment retailer Heinnie Haynes is also a multi-tool convert. He appreciated having one for quick fixes while renovating his cottage, and particularly rates the needle-nose pliers, which rival standard models rather than acting as an emergency substitute.

Kilburn suggests multi-tools can be a useful starting point for someone who doesn’t own a toolbox, and at the other end of the spectrum are the tinkerers and prepared problem-solvers Emanuel sees as natural fits.

“The person who will value a Leatherman is the one who spends their after-hours in the garage building stuff that they probably never need, it’s the kind of self-reliant and prepared person who you rely on to solve a problem,” Emanuel says.

The Leatherman Wave+ currently costs $129.95, meaning it should be a well-considered purchase rather than an impulse buy.

It’s reassuring to know that you’ll be investing in a refined product designed because of a genuine practical need. Founder Tim Leatherman conceived a pliers-based multi-tool after encountering car and plumbing problems while traveling through Europe in the 1970s, and after careful development, he launched the original Pocket Survival Tool in 1983.

Today you’re paying for that established reputation and durable construction, and Leatherman backs its products with a 25-year warranty.

“They’re ridiculously well built, really well regarded, and their choice of tools is good,” Emanuel says. He describes sought-after Leathermans as the “collectible top end of the multi-tool market.”

Kilburn recalls seeing lower-priced multi-tools failing his comrades during their military career. “Some disintegrate over time because they were just cheaply made with poor-quality material [and] poor-quality steel,” he says. His Leatherman Surge, meanwhile, has lasted over 20 years. If replacing it again, he says he would choose Leatherman over his backup Gerber multi-tool because he prefers its feel and durability.

Leatherman makes a wide range of multi-tools, so it pays to consider which functions you’ll genuinely use. The Signal model adds outdoor-focused features suited to camping, including a ferrocerium rod, emergency whistle and sharpener, but omits scissors. I use scissors enough for plant pruning, first aid and gear repairs that the Wave+ remains the better fit for me.

If you’re unlikely to use most of its functions, a smaller, cheaper multi-tool could make more sense. The Wave+ is also heavier than minimalist models, and there’s a learning curve when figuring out where everything lives.

Don’t forget that a premium multi-tool only represents good value if you look after it. We remove dirt after outdoor adventures and dry and lubricate it before storing. We also avoid forcing it to tackle jobs better suited to full-size tools. I wouldn’t, for example, choose its compact saw over a dedicated full-size version for pruning substantial tree branches in my yard.

If you’re using a Wave+ in the UK, like me, be aware of the country’s knife laws. You need a “good reason” to carry it in public because its blades lock. However, Emanuel explains that the legal language is ambiguous, so you shouldn’t assume you can carry one wherever you go just because it’s part of a multi-tool.

The Wave+ has convinced me that a good multi-tool is more than merely an expensive gimmick. It may not replace dedicated tools, but having so many functions at my fingertips in a form that is so compact, portable and easy to use makes it a practical, worthwhile investment.

The Wave Plus is a multi-tool workhorse. It packs 18 tools in one, including sharp blades, spring scissors, wire cutters, and more.

#7803. This Trending Home Feature Is More Practical Than Pretty

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 8, 2026 11:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Each year, Zonda publishes an annual Cost vs. Value (CVV) report, ranking the most common home renovation projects across the nation by return on investment (ROI) value. For the first time, backup power generators entered the top 10 ranking on the list at number 7, with ROI exceeding 100 percent in hurricane-prone and storm-affected regions.

We wanted to understand why home backup power is more popular than ever, since it’s long been considered a luxury upgrade as opposed to an essential part of modern home preparedness. Here’s what several home generator experts and real estate pros think are the reasons why homeowners and homebuyers are now prioritizing backup power and whole-home generators when it comes to home value.

Before we dive into the reasons more people are opting to have a standby generator or whole-home backup generator, it’s important to understand exactly what it does and how it functions. Permanently installed outside a home, a standby generator produces enough electricity to power an entire house indefinitely in the event of a power outage. It connects directly to the home’s electrical panel and uses the natural gas line for fuel. One of the major benefits is that a standby generator automatically turns on within seconds of the power going out, seamlessly transferring the power source from the grid to the generator.

A portable generator is a gas-powered machine that you can carry or wheel over short distances. It has outlets so you can power several appliances. However, it only functions as a temporary power source when the electricity shuts off, making it less reliable than a standby generator. It’s also noisier, requires setup each time you use it, and needs to be refueled periodically.

This whole-home standby generator features a dual-fuel design and a transfer switch that automatically kicks on when the power goes out.

A rise in storm frequency and severity plays a role in more people wanting a backup generator for their home. “Outages stopped feeling rare,” says Beau Tyrrel, product training manager at Jackery. “The average U.S. customer lost about 11 hours of power in 2024, nearly double the decade before. When something happens twice as often, people start planning for it.”

Bert Woidan, operations manager at Trademark Electric, a Generac PowerPro Prestige dealer in Ocala, Florida, recognizes how generator sales are a storm-driven market. “I believe with the increase in weather-related power outages, it only makes sense that more homeowners would want a backup generator with their home,” he explains. “When our company first started selling generators over 20 years ago, I remember standing in the parking lot talking with our founder, and we set a goal to install at least one generator a week. Today, we order generators by the semi load, and during a busy storm season, we’re installing two to three generators a day.”

More storms mean more stress over potential damage. “Especially in our region, if you lose power, the biggest concern is your AC going out,” notes Woidan. “With how humid it gets, it’s not just uncomfortable, but the humidity and moisture can damage your home very quickly, so it’s super important to keep your AC running even if you lose power.”

In the Midwest, the big fear is the basement, says Omar Muhammad, owner of Excel Electrical Technologies in Orland Park, Illinois. “Most homes in our area have a sump pump, and the storms that knock out power are the same storms that send water toward your foundation.” A finished basement can take on tens of thousands of dollars of damage in one night if the pump stops, so buyers and residents understand that a generator protects the most expensive square footage in their house.

Technological innovation has been a game changer for how Americans live. Homes depend on electricity in ways they didn’t 20 years ago, says Muhammad. “A lot of people work from home now and some run medical equipment. Many have an EV in the garage; a high-efficiency furnace that won’t run without power; and a smart thermostat, security system, and Wi-Fi network they rely on every day,” he explains. “An outage is a lot different than it used to be—now it can mean you can’t work, can’t heat the house, and can’t charge your car.” Therefore, a standby generator has become a non-negotiable addition for many homeowners who can’t afford to have their power shut off for any period of time.

Standby generators are now recognized as being as necessary as smoke detectors and security systems, adding value to a home. According to Briggs & Stratton, a permanently installed generator could get you a 3 to 5 percent boost to your home value. And they are now more widespread and becoming the norm, so buyers expect to see them. “Most new builds automatically include a backup generator installation in the blueprints,” notes Woidan.

From a resale perspective, a home generator can help a property stand out by offering buyers peace of mind, especially in neighborhoods that have experienced repeated power disruptions, says Dell Jeanty, founder of Dell Residential Group in Arlington, Virginia. “A home with a generator during an outage demonstrates preparedness, which can be a meaningful selling point,” says Jeanty. “Some estimates suggest standby generators can recover as much as 95 percent of their installation cost at resale, although the actual return depends on the market, installation costs, and buyer demand.”

Curb Appeal Updates You’ll Appreciate Even If You Aren’t Selling Your Home

Curb appeal does not have to be solely cosmetic. See which good-looking projects we are prioritizing to make homes safer, more energy-efficient, and weather resistant.

#7802. May Court Order Parent to "Immediately Cease All Disparagement of" Other Parent "via Social Media"?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

An appellate court orders a trial court to consider whether such an order is consistent with the First Amendment.

From McWilliams v. Meghrian, decided Monday by Georgia Court of Appeals Judges Jeffrey Watkins, Christopher McFadden, and J. Wade Padgett:

This appeal arises from a child custody modification proceeding in which the trial court, [among other things,] … permanently enjoined … Mother … from making any "disparaging" statements about Father "via social media or other means" and modified child support. Mother appeals, and for the reasons below, we vacate the trial court's final order and remand for further proceedings. The parties are the parents of one child, born in 2008….

Mother argues that the final order and accompanying parenting plan included unconstitutional prior restraints on speech. The final order directed Mother to "immediately cease all disparagement of [Father] whether via social media or other means." The final order also adopted and incorporated the parenting plan proposed by Father, which provided that the parties "will not speak badly of each other or the members of the family of the other parent." …

During the final hearing, the trial court stated, "So, Ms. McWilliams, when we're dealing with, you know, parents—and I understand what you said. You're putting your truth out there and saying your truth. Disparagement doesn't care about the truth. It just means that you're putting down another parent." Mother responded, "Yeah." The court concluded:

And so publicly like that is something that you just—you can't do, and so we want to be careful about that. There's a reason that we're careful about that. Things on social media get back to kids. They just do. And I think that we're all—we're all cognizant of that in this day and age, but we have to be careful about what we put out there. And if we can't say anything nice, we just don't need to say anything at all, and that's the best rule to live by in terms of this. So that's—that's kind of what we need to—what we need to work on there….

As to Mother's failure to assert her constitutional challenge before the trial court, it is true that "[b]ecause this Court is a court for the correction of errors, we will not consider matters, even of constitutional magnitude, that were not raised and ruled upon in the trial court." However, the injunction, in its objectionable form, was not entered until the final order. And Mother raised the issue in her application for discretionary review, which was her first opportunity to do so.

Accordingly, on remand, the trial court is instructed to address the constitutional issue in the first instance. As we do not reach the constitutional issue, we need not decide whether, as Father argues, it is moot because the child has reached 18 years of age…. In sum, we vacate the grant of attorney fees, the injunction (both in the final order and in the incorporated parenting plan) restricting speech, and the order of child support….

Malone Williams Allen represents the mother.

#7801. 8 Reasons a Contractor Might Give You an Outrageously High Estimate

If you just got a quote for a home repair that made your eyes water, there's probably a reason it's so high. A team of contractors weighs in with possible explanations.

If you just got a quote from a contractor that was way more than you thought it would be, join the club…it happens to the best of us. In fact, it’s a pretty common occurrence. Sometimes, though, the quote is so high that you can feel your mouth forming words you shouldn’t be saying. As someone who has been on both sides of such interactions, I can say that contractors don’t like them any more than you do. They know you can shop around, and they need your business. So what’s the deal with ridiculously high quotes?

I didn’t find any shortage of contractors willing to weigh in on this topic — one that is near and dear to their professional hearts. If a quote just made you hyperventilate, take a deep breath and check out some of the possible reasons why it’s so much higher than you expected.

“If an HVAC unit has a defective part that needs replacement, most of my clients will immediately ask how much the replacement part costs,” says HVAC technician Tamer Sayed. “I always tell the current market price and the misunderstanding often starts here. A few clients forget to take into account the labor and consultation fees. They assume they only had to pay for the replacement part.”

The same thing can happen with plumbing and electrical jobs. The part needed to get things working again may be small and inexpensive, and it may only account for a small portion of the quote. Sometimes the labor quote seems excessive, and that’s usually because the client doesn’t understand what’s involved with the repair.

Jake Vincett, a builder from the UK, makes this observation: “A lot of the time, the customer is comparing quotes for different work, because the cheaper one has included a surface repair whereas the more expensive one has quoted for fixing the underlying problem…It’s common that the customer doesn’t know or consider the amount of work going into a project. A new driveway isn’t just laying tarmac – it’s digging out the old one, laying the sub base, etc.”

Plumbing, electrical and HVAC expert Bob Cardwell adds: “It’s often not only one problem to fix but a bunch of small fixes. Even though it might be possible to fix the original problem without addressing the additional issues, an experienced and reliable technician will not ignore them, will try to fix them and will discuss them with the homeowner.”

Failing to provide a quote that addresses underlying issues and then delivering a sky-high bill at the end doesn’t just make the customer unhappy, says HVAC and plumbing expert Ryan Osterkamp. “It can make them feel like we don’t know what we’re doing.”

Osterkamp is used to hearing customers say: “I can go get that part for $X at Home Depot.” What they aren’t thinking about is the amount of training and expertise that made it possible for our technician to quickly and accurately diagnose the issue, have the supplies they need in their truck and be able to do the repair same day. Sure, you may save money by going with the guy on Facebook that works out of an old, unlabeled truck, but if his work doesn’t hold up, will he fix it without giving you the runaround? Is he insured? Does he offer a warranty?”

Tariffs, inflation and the economy in general are pushing prices up, and the dollar has lost a lot of its purchasing power for the average American. The same is true for contractors. “The fact of the matter is, we’re working harder now and making less,” says remodeling contractor Kevin Cullen. “In today’s economy, a lot of people are chasing the price to the bottom and shopping for the cheapest number. Unfortunately, they usually get what they pay for.”

A contractor who knows problems might creep up, such as a rotten subfloor that needs replacement during a toilet repair, makes an effort to warn customers as part of the quote. Potential problems aren’t always obvious. “There are times,” says Nika Tveretinova, who operates an HVAC business in Sacramento, “when the actual fix isn’t that complicated, but it’s the access that makes things tough—especially with equipment installed in an attic or cramped quarters. Sometimes we also find an old installation that needs a safety or code correction before we can put everything back together.”

In such situations, a higher-than-expected quote that you can reject is far better than a higher-than-expected bill you have to pay because the work is already completed.

Joshua Kurz founded NumeralQ, a home improvement pricing guide, and he cautions against comparing a bid you receive from a contractor to information you find online. “Owners often find an estimate online, and rather than waiting for a bid, they assume that number will be the actual cost. These estimates are helpful when determining a budget, but they are not interchangeable for actual bids. A 1,500 sq ft roof in one market will not necessarily cost the same in another market, and bids can even differ for neighboring houses.”

If you find a guy on Facebook who charges a low price to do a repair, there’s no guarantee that the repair will last or be up to code. When that person makes a mistake, a licensed contractor working on the same system at a later date might have to fix it, especially when inspectors are involved.

“Over a 40-year career,” says Cullen, “I’ve found many surprises: unsupported headers, no king or jack studs, undersized headers, poorly installed headers that aren’t flush and have gaps, termite damage, carpenter ant damage, water damage, mold. That’s not every job, but you never know when a homeowner bought a house in which a Rube Goldberg did the work on it.”

Sometimes a house is in such poor condition that a small repair, such as stopping a plumbing leak, can turn into a major project that involves replacing pipes, walls or subfloors. Rather than simply declining the repair, some contractors will offer a ridiculously high quote to avoid falling into a sinkhole of extra work. If the customer accepts the quote, the contractor won’t lose money by taking the job. A customer who rejects a bid can keep shopping with no harm done.

#7800. How Trump's Undermining of the Constitution Helped Cause a "Blue Tsunami"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Trump's unconstitutional policies on tariffs, the Iran War, and immigration played a big role in his party's enormous "Blue Tsunami" election defeat.

On Tuesday, Trump and the Republican suffered a massive electoral defeat, losing control of both houses of Congress. Many have called it a "Blue Tsunami". The defeat was caused by multiple factors. But Trump's unconstitutional actions on tariffs, the War in Iran, and immigration played a major role. Violations of the Constitution don't always result in political setbacks for the perpetrators. But in this case they did "bigly." As Texas GOP Senator Ted Cruz put it, "Tariffs have made everything too expensive, and the Iran war has dragged on too long."

This connection is perhaps most obvious in the case of tariffs. Since returning to power in January 2025, Trump has engaged in a series of massive tariff power grabs, repeatedly attempting to usurp congressional authority in this field, and use it to impose the highest tariff schedule since the Great Depression. He started with the IEEPA tariffs. When the Supreme Court invalidated them, he tried again with Section 122 and Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, and the Section 338 tariffs against Canada. In each case, he illegally tried to transform relatively narrow delegations to the executive into a blank check to impose tariffs at will. The net effect of these actions has been to raise prices for consumers,  reduce economic growth, and impose some $700 billion in new taxes on Americans over a 10-year period (unless courts end up striking down the new tariffs, too). The tariffs also failed to produce the promised increase manufacturing employment.

Most relevant for present purposes, affordability and price increases were clearly a huge issue in the election. And most voters have come to realize that tariffs increase prices, and damage the economy. Exit polls reveal that 66% of voters believe Trump's tariffs have hurt the national economy (compared to only 21% who believe they helped), and a similar percentage (64%) believe they hurt the economy in their area (only 14% believe they helped it). Numerous other polls show widespread opposition to the tariffs, as well (e.g. here and here). They became a major issue in the elections, linked to the broader issues of price increases and "affordability."

Polls, pundits, and even Donald Trump and Vice President J.D. Vance all agree the Iran War was a major factor in GOP losses. The military stalemate combined with resulting energy price increases have enraged voters. Exit polls showed that 74% of voters said the war was a "crucial" or "important" factor in their decisions, and the vast majority of them disapproved of Trump's conduct of it.

And, as I have argued from the beginning, that war is unconstitutional because it was never authorized by Congress.  As I warned at the start of the conflict, the failure to build up the public supported needed to secure congressional authorization greatly reduced the odds of success:

This [constitutional] limitation on presidential power is more than just a technical legal point. The requirement of congressional authorization for the initiation of war is there to ensure that no one person can take the country to war on his own, and that any major military actions have broad public support, which can be essential to ensuring that we have the will and commitment needed to achieve victory against difficult opponents. Trump's failure to seek and secure that kind of broad public support has ensured that only about 27 percent of Americans approve of this military action, compared to 43 percent who disapprove, according to a Reuters poll. Other surveys show similar results. This is a historically low level of public support at the start of a major military action and bodes ill for U.S. staying power if we suffer reverses or a prolonged conflict results.

I think that prediction has (so far at least) been vindicated by events.

The immigration situation is somewhat more complicated than that with tariffs and war. But, here too, various unconstitutional actions have damaged the GOP's political standing and hurt the party in the election. Trump's cruel mass deportation policies have made ICE by far the most the most unpopular federal agency (surpassing even the IRS) and alienated Hispanic voters in Texas and elsewhere;  this was a key factor in the Republicans' defeat in that state. GOP immigration policies  led many Hispanics who backed Trump and the GOP in 2024 to turn against them in 2026.

In part because of indefensible double standards in relevant Supreme Court precedent, courts permit a wide range of harsh and cruel conduct in immigration policy, that would be invalidated in any other context. But many of Trump's policies went beyond even these overly permissive bounds. As a result, the administration has lost many thousands of immigration detention and deportation cases, including many on constitutional grounds, and many before GOP-appointed judges. Trump's immigration crackdown has violated the Constitution in various other ways, as well, as in the case of his use of an absurdly broad definition of "invasion" in order to justify detaining and deporting even legal migrants without due process.

In all three of these cases, voter backlash arose primarily because of the awful - and highly visible - practical consequences, rather than because of the constitutional issues themselves. Most voters care far more about military failure, rising prices, and visible cruelty of these policies than about their legality. Nonetheless, it is still true that unconstitutional conduct played a major role in causing the tsunami that swept away many GOP officeholders.

We should not be overly optimistic about this chain of events.  It would be a mistake to assume that unconstitutional policies always lead to electoral punishment, or even usually do so. In many cases, voters are unaware of illegality or don't give it much weight if they do find out. Previous presidents have often avoided significant political backlash for violating the Constitution. Barack Obama, for example, also waged two unconstitutional wars (those against Libya and ISIS). But because the wars were (at least initially) militarily successful, led to few casualties, and had little visible negative economic impact, he largely avoided political damage. Later, Obama concluded that the Libya war was his worst mistake. But Democrats didn't pay much, if any, political price for it.

Trump's unconstitutional actions on these three issues turned out be politically costly because the negative effects were large and highly visible. Even many generally ignorant and inattentive voters noticed them.

Here, as always, I do not claim that public support for my position somehow proves I was right. As the author of Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, I recognize that majority public opinion is heavily influenced by ignorance and bias, and thus often a poor guide to goo policy. Moreover, while majority opinion agrees with me in condemning Trump's policies here, it would not go as far as I would in sweeping away nearly all tariffs and immigration restrictions.

Despite these caveats, I am glad that the public punished the GOP for these terrible unconstitutional policies. I hope this outcome might deter future presidents from imitating them. At the very least, they might hesitate to pursue them on the same massive scale as Trump did.

City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#7799. Justice Department Announces Results from Operation Not Forgotten 2026

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Department of Justice and FBI announced today results of the personnel surge in support of Operation Not Forgotten 2026, which focuses on unresolved cases in Indian country with a priority on cases involving violence against women and children, including those who are missing or murdered.

In its fourth year, Operation Not Forgotten surged personnel and investigative resources across the country from April 1 through September 30, resulting in 118 arrests, 41 individuals charged federally, 25 child victims identified or located, and 72 weapons recovered.  FBI agents conducted 990 interviews and 232 search operations.  Arrests increased by 123% and subjects charged by 52% over 2025.

“The Department of Justice will always work to deliver justice for the victims of violent crime in Indian country,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Thanks to the hard work of the FBI, our U.S. Attorneys, and other federal and tribal partners, Operation Not Forgotten and Operation Steadfast Promise are helping make communities safer and providing comfort for victims and families.”

“This year’s Operation Not Forgotten continued this FBI’s largest commitment to Indian Country in the history of the Bureau,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “The results were outstanding – from April 1 through September 30, this FBI worked more than 500 cases, a 59% increase from last year’s operation; 118 arrests, a 123% increase; and 41 subjects charged federally, a 52% increase. This is in addition to 25 child victims identified or located and 72 weapons recovered. These involved life-saving operations, with cases including child sexual abuse, physical assault and abuse, domestic violence, CSAM cases, and more.

“Operation Not Forgotten sends a loud and clear message that our long-forgotten partners in Indian Country are forgotten no more,” said Director Patel. “When I assumed the position of FBI Director a year and a half ago, this FBI promised we would be there for our tribal partners. We have and will continue to be – through our 400 agents dedicated to Indian country, 30 Safe Trails Task Forces, and increased awareness with our Voices Not Forgotten program, where the FBI quadrupled the rewards to at least $25,000 for information associated with homicides, kidnappings and missing persons in Indian country. Thank you to our federal, state, and local partners who continue to work with us to ensure these unsolved crimes and cases receive the surge in resources they deserve.”

“Operation Not Forgotten demonstrates the Trump Administration’s commitment to protecting tribal communities, strengthening public safety, and ensuring that victims and their families have access to justice,” said Billy Kirkland, Assistant Secretary for Indian Affairs, U.S. Department of the Interior. “Through close collaboration across the federal government and in partnership with tribal, state, and local law enforcement, we are bringing additional resources and investigative support to Indian Country to address violent crime, advance unresolved cases, and help families find answers. The Department of the Interior, through the Bureau of Indian Affairs, remains committed to working alongside our partners to deliver meaningful results and build safer communities for generations to come."

Examples of cases charged during this period include:

In the District of Wyoming, the surge resulted in the federal indictment of 18 individuals for an array of violent crimes, and child abuse offenses on the Wind River Indian Reservation, including U.S. v. Jose Benito Ocon: This prosecution arises from an August 2025 incident near Riverton, where the defendant allegedly executed a male passenger with a gunshot to the head inside a moving vehicle before turning the firearm on two female witnesses.  Leveraging the surge’s enhanced investigative assets, a grand jury returned an indictment charging the defendant with five felony counts, including first-degree murder, discharging a firearm during a crime of violence, and two distinct counts of assault with a dangerous weapon. He faces a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment if convicted.  In U.S. v. Darlynn Sheree Seminole, federal prosecutors filed charges following a June 2026 domestic violence intervention by the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Wind River Police Department, involving allegations of severe physical trauma inflicted on a 10-year-old.

In the District of Nevada, in July a federal grand jury returned a superseding indictment charging Delshay Astor with the alleged murder of Anna Scott, a member of the Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe, on the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony in February 2022, and also charged Joel Christy for assisting Astor to avoid apprehension.

In the District of Minnesota, Operation Not Forgotten has resulted in four cases charged during the surge period with violent and sexual offenses in Indian Country, including sexual abuse of minors, domestic assault causing substantial bodily injury, assault by strangulation, and assault with intent to commit kidnapping. One recent case includes U.S. v. Courtney John Barrett Sr. indicted on September 22, 2026, on two counts of sexual abuse of a minor.

In the District of Montana, Michael Plentybuffalo was charged in the death of Shann Nomee, who went missing during an extreme cold snap in January 2024 and whose frozen body was found in a field north of Lodge Grass, Montana after a community led search and a tip to the Bureau of Indian Affairs that pointed to Plentybuffalo.  His case is pending trial.

Also in Montana, Lance Crookedarm was charged with the May 2026 violent assault and non-fatal strangulation of a female victim.

In the District of Arizona, at least four cases were charged including two violent assaults, an arson, and the aggravated sexual abuse of a minor under 12, all of which occurred on the Navajo Nation, as well as an additional assault that was committed on the Fort Apache Indian Reservation.

Operation Steadfast Promise, first announced in 2026, is a continuing comprehensive surge of resources to address a wide range of violent criminal threats impacting Indian country. Operation Steadfast Promise builds on the successes of Operation Not Forgotten with the addition of multiple new initiatives to improve public safety in Tribal communities. The FBI, in coordination with U.S. Attorneys’ Offices, the Bureau of Indian Affairs Missing and Murdered Unit, Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and Tribal and other federal law enforcement partners, is working across multiple territories to bring investigative aid to cases and resolution for victims and their families. Since Operation Steadfast Promise began in April, the FBI opened over 1,200 new investigations in Indian country, obtained criminal charges on 678 subjects, made over 700 arrests, recovered 2,260 weapons, and made 140 drug seizures.

This year, Operation Not Forgotten continued to address the over 4,000 open investigations in Indian country including death investigations, child abuse cases, domestic violence, and adult sexual abuse investigations, underscoring the persistent and urgent need for sustained resource investment in these communities.

During Operation Not Forgotten, the FBI surged personnel, including investigative, intelligence, and other support personnel, on rotating temporary duty assignments across Indian country in twelve FBI field offices, in Albuquerque, Billings, Detroit, Denver, Jackson, Las Vegas, Minneapolis, Oklahoma City, Omaha, Portland, Phoenix and Salt Lake City. Working in close coordination with Tribal law enforcement agencies, the BIA Missing and Murdered Unit, and U.S. Attorneys' Offices, together law enforcement worked to advance open investigations and pursue accountability for victims and their families.

Additionally, the FBI has brought focus to a new FBI’s Voices Not Forgotten webpage that includes a searchable and interactive map that brings attention to FBI investigations in Indian country where the FBI, in coordination with state, local and Tribal law enforcement are seeking the public’s assistance. In August 2026, the FBI announced the establishment of a new protocol which created a minimum reward of up to $25,000 for all publicly advertised cases involving homicides, kidnappings and missing persons in Indian country where the FBI has assumed jurisdiction.

The FBI remains committed to standing alongside Tribal communities, federal partners, and local law enforcement to address the violent crime threats that continue to impact Indian country. To learn more, visit www.fbi.gov/investigate/violent-crime/indian-country-crime.

The FBI encourages anyone with information related to unresolved violent crimes in Indian country to contact their local FBI field office or submit a tip at https://tips.fbi.gov.

#7798. Declaratory Judgment + $275K in Attorney Fees in Settlement of N.H. "XX" Wristbands Case

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The Institute for Free Speech, which litigated the case, reports on the settlement agreement:

Take off the wristbands or leave. That was the message Bow school officials gave parents and a grandfather who were silently protesting in support of female-only sports by wearing pink "XX" wristbands at a girls' high school soccer game in 2024…. After more than two years of litigation …, the Bow School District has agreed to a judgment declaring that it violated the plaintiffs' rights by barring them from wearing the wristbands at the game. U.S…. The settlement also provides $275,000 in attorneys' fees and costs.

The judgment declares that the plaintiffs "have a First Amendment right to silently wear pink wristbands bearing the XX symbol on the sidelines, in the spectator's area, or in the parking lot of any Bow District sporting event." It binds the district and its Board of Education, and it remains in effect even if the district amends its policies….

The plaintiffs wore the wristbands, whose "XX" symbols reference female chromosome structure, to protest a policy permitting a biological male to compete on the opposing girls' team. School officials, accompanied by a police officer, confronted them. The referee halted play until one spectator removed his wristband, and school officials later issued trespass orders barring Fellers and Andy Foote from school grounds, preventing them from attending their children's games and other school activities for a time….

After the district court denied a preliminary injunction in April 2025, the plaintiffs appealed. In August 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit ruled in the plaintiffs' favor, finding that they "have established a likelihood of success as to their viewpoint discrimination claim." The court concluded that the protest "fell short of harassment and disruption," and that school officials "cannot favor one side of a debate involving parental speech on an issue of prominent public concern." …

Here's my August post excerpting the First Circuit's opinion, written by First Circuit Judge Sandra Lynch, joined by Judge Jeffrey Howard:

On September 17, 2024, [plaintiffs] were instructed by Bow High School officials to remove pink "XX" wristbands they wore in protest while watching their daughters (in [one plaintiff's] case, granddaughter) play in a girls' soccer game against a team with one transgender athlete. Further sanctions followed…. [W]e conclude that appellants have established a likelihood of success as to their viewpoint discrimination claim arising from the sanctions imposed on them for their passive speech in wearing these wristbands….

The district court analyzed the school playing fields and adjacent parking lot, as appellants requested, under the mode of First Amendment law applicable to limited public fora as to impermissible viewpoint discrimination…. [The] appellee school district argues that this case must be analyzed more in the mode of Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District (1969) … [and other cases that] recognize the particular interests inherent in the public elementary and high school settings, and the necessary discretion given to public school administrators in the difficult job of running public schools….

Neither of those two different classic modes of First Amendment analysis, urged on by these opposing parties, is a perfect fit for this public high school speech case, and we note that the Supreme Court has not addressed this precise question. We need not and do not reach the complex question of which (or whether) either of these alternate modes is the appropriate First Amendment type of analytical model for the facts of record here. We conclude that on these facts the differences in analysis would not affect the outcome here….

The school's legitimate interest in regulating certain kinds of speech on the playing field sidelines … is not demonstrated by the evidence in this record. There is no evidence that appellants' protest caused a material disruption [which would be relevant under Tinker]. There was no disruption until school officials chose to intervene, after which the referee suspended the game for approximately fifteen minutes and the school officials chose to impose restrictions on appellants' speech and impose sanctions. The appellants did not stage any pregame demonstrations; did not march, shout, chant, or otherwise disrupt the game; and did not confront Tirrell or any other player. Instead, they waited until halftime before donning the "XX" wristbands in a passive, silent gesture of protest. There is also no evidence of harassment, given there is no evidence in the record that any player actually saw the wristbands.

The lack of any evidence demonstrating harassment also defeats the school district's argument that it had an affirmative duty under Title IX to protect students from the speech in which appellants engaged…. While it is true that appellants chose to protest at the September 17 game because of Tirrell being a player, the record does not contain evidence of appellants engaging in harassment before or during the game. To the contrary, appellants did not shout, chant, make threats, or aggressively gesture at Tirrell to communicate their views against her participation. Nor is there evidence that Tirrell or any other player even saw the wristbands or "subjectively perceived the environment to be hostile or abusive."

Principal Fisk did note the challenges that transgender students face generally. But Fisk did not ever explain how appellants' display of the "XX" symbol constituted sufficiently severe or pervasive conduct to qualify as harassment under Title IX. And to the extent the district court concluded that the silent wearing of "XX" wristbands on the sidelines of a school soccer field, without more, always amounts to harassing speech, we disagree.

The school district responds that it may make "predictive judgment[s]" to proactively prohibit conduct that it believes will eventually lead to an actionable Title IX claim….. We agree with the general proposition. But the argument fails on the facts of this record…. We need not decide in this appeal whether and under what circumstances passive speech, on other facts, consisting of displaying the "XX" symbol on school property during school events could be reasonably thought to be harassing. But appellants' silent display of the "XX" symbol at the September 17 game fell short of harassment and disruption, and we conclude that the district court erred in holding that the school's interest in prevention of harassment justified the prohibition.

While it is a closer issue, we conclude that the school district likely was not justified in sanctioning the appellants for their passive speech based on its concerns derived from the earlier exchanges with the appellants and other parents. None of appellants' reported discussions, including their possible different methods of protest reported to Bow High School officials by other parents, led to any attempt to "heckle and intimidate" Tirrell. And that was evident both before and throughout the game.

It is true that Fellers initially attempted to convince his daughter to get the Bow High School players to wear the wristbands, but his daughter informed him that "she could not get full support from the team and was afraid that it would divide them." Fellers's Facebook post made the night before the game encouraged spectators "to protect the integrity and safety of female athletics" and "come out to support our XX Lady Falcons and show your solidarity with our girls' team." But the record shows only that the appellants and perhaps others of similar views engaged in a passive protest and only started the protest at halftime. While the school district may make predictive judgments about whether disruption may occur and "need not be certain of its forecast," it cannot use those projections to immediately suppress a passive, silent protest, that did not impair any of the legitimate school administration interests recognized by the Supreme Court.

This brings us to the school officials' other stated reasons for sanctioning appellants. Superintendent Kelley stated that the "XX" symbol conveyed an "exclusionary" message about gender. Principal Fisk, who ordered appellants to remove the wristbands, described the symbol both as "hateful" and as "anti-trans." As to these justifications for the sanctions imposed, the record evidence demonstrates the likelihood that the school district imposed sanctions on the appellants' wearing of the wristbands because it disagreed with the protest message conveyed….

Although the leading Supreme Court case on viewpoint discrimination in academic limited public fora, involved colleges and not high schools, and involved a limited public forum, both significant differences, Rosenberger's anguage about viewpoint discrimination is pertinent. "The government must abstain from regulating speech when the specific motivating ideology or the opinion or perspective of the speaker is the rationale for the restriction."

The characteristics of the school as a place of learning reinforce that administrators cannot favor one side of a debate involving parental speech on an issue of prominent public concern, and which, in those parents' views, concerned the safety of their children. As the Supreme Court stated in a case involving a high school football game, "learning how to tolerate diverse expressive activities has always been 'part of learning how to live in a pluralistic society.'"

Judge Julie Rikelman concurred in the judgment, reasoning that Tinker might not prohibit viewpoint-discriminatory speech restrictions, but that in this case the school district had accepted the viewpoint neutrality requirement:

The school district accepted that the limited public forum framework applied to the facts here and conceded repeatedly, both in its brief and at oral argument, that it could restrict speech at the September 17 soccer game only for viewpoint neutral reasons…. Although it did urge us to conduct our First Amendment analysis with the principles of Tinker in mind, it did so only in arguing that its actions were reasonable and thus satisfied the [reasonableness] prong of the limited public forum test….

With the school district's concession in mind, I agree that the record lacks evidence of actionable harassment or material disruption from the plaintiffs' speech at the September 17 soccer game. The record also demonstrates that school officials likely restricted the XX symbol because they viewed it as "exclusionary" and demeaning to transgender students. That amounts to viewpoint discrimination under relevant precedent.

Del Kolde, Brett Nolan, and Nathan Ristuccia (Institute for Free Speech) and Richard Lehmann (Lehmann Major List, PLLC) represent plaintiffs. were on brief, for appellants.

#7797. How to Thaw the Frozen Housing Market

Today’s housing market is painful for just about everyone involved, from builders to buyers to sellers. Government failures over the last seven years froze the industry and made homeownership less affordable, but the problem could be solved if Congress would act. 

To understand the solution, though, we first must know how we got here.

Beginning in 2020, Congress increased annual spending by trillions of dollars, and the Federal Reserve simply created the money to cover the massive deficits. The Fed also pushed interest rates to near zero and bought mortgage-backed securities (MBS).

The low interest rates made it cheaper for the government to borrow, but also for everyone else to borrow, including would-be homebuyers. Lower mortgage rates allowed people to take on much larger mortgages without making monthly mortgage payments prohibitively expensive. The resulting bidding wars sent home prices to stratospheric levels.

Fed purchases of MBS were fuel on the fire. They incentivized banks to make more loans at lower interest rates, stimulating mortgage lending. That’s precisely why the Fed bought MBS for the first time in the wake of the mortgage meltdown in 2009—it was attempting to rescue the industry. This time, the Fed bought MBS from early 2020 through early 2022.

The result was even larger mortgages from even lower interest rates as home prices went to the moon. Additionally, the runaway spending, borrowing, and printing of money by the government devalued the dollar and sent inflation to 40-year highs. The weaker dollar also meant it took more of those dollars to buy the same home, further inflating prices, but it also caused the Fed to change course.

>>> Government Broke the Housing Market—Only This Will Fix It

What followed was the sharpest rise in interest rates in four decades. Suddenly, mortgage rates were three or four times their previous levels. Ordinarily, higher interest rates would put downward pressure on home prices so that monthly mortgage payments stay roughly the same, but that didn’t happen.

If you bought a home in 2020 with a 2 percent interest rate mortgage, you effectively can’t sell your home today, not without downsizing. If you sell today, your old mortgage gets paid off and your next mortgage will have an interest rate closer to 8 percent. You can’t borrow anywhere near as much on the next home, or your monthly mortgage payment will explode.

These golden handcuffs have kept many existing homes off the market and even those that are for sale have unrealistically high prices. Sellers want those high prices so they’ll have more money to put down on their next home and therefore need to borrow less. That makes the higher interest rate much less painful and keeps the monthly mortgage payment manageable.

But that’s left a massive mismatch between buyers and sellers. Would-be buyers can’t afford today’s high prices with today’s high interest rates. Homeownership affordability is near an all-time low because it takes 44% of the median household pre-tax income to afford a median-price home. The after-tax figure is well over 50 percent.

Consequently, pending sales of existing homes have fallen to the lowest level on record, a full one-third below the level from a quarter century ago.

>>> U.S. Government-Backed Homebuying Market Drives Up House Prices for Ordinary Americans  

The situation is painful for new homes too. Residential construction is trending down, and homebuilder sentiment has fallen to the lowest level in 14 years. Builders are being squeezed by costs 60% higher than before the pandemic, and buyers who can’t afford today’s prices. About two-thirds of builders are using sales incentives to clear inventory, with more than 40 percent cutting prices.

For transactions to increase and the housing market to clear, home prices ultimately need to come down relative to incomes, which will take time because sellers need to adjust their expectations. But lower interest rates would also give buyers some relief and reduce the lock-in effect on current homeowners looking to sell. 

That’s where Congress needs to act. The legislature has no direct control over interest rates, but they do control spending, which is at obscene levels. In the last fiscal year, which just ended on September 30, the federal government spent $7.4 trillion and had to borrow almost $2 trillion of it.

Everyone, including the government, competes for loans and that additional $2 trillion of competition drives up the price to borrow money, which is the interest rate. Reducing government spending would reduce the deficit and immediately put downward pressure on interest rates, including for mortgages.

Granted, other recent factors have contributed to higher interest rates—like the Iran war increasing oil prices, which increase inflation expectations, which increase interest rates. Ending that conflict would help stabilize energy markets and eventually reduce interest rates too. But it’s the spending that’s squarely within Congress’s control and which would have a faster impact.

But given the abundance of ineptitude and lack of fortitude within the halls of Congress, don’t expect those spending cuts anytime soon.

#7794. Blocking Data Centers at Home Could Put Americans’ Data at Risk Abroad

If artificial intelligence (AI) companies are boxed out of every jurisdiction in the United States, they may need to locate their infrastructure offshore instead. That may resolve not-in-my-backyard concerns and prevent utility rates from increasing—at least from data centers—but it presents other disadvantages that AI’s opponents are likely overlooking.

The most obvious is the economic loss caused by pushing out a booming industry. Another is losing autonomy over Americans’ data.

Why Offshore Data Centers Put Americans’ Data at Risk

Consider what happens to U.S. data that relies on infrastructure in countries that do not share our value of freedom of speech. Our data could be subject to the same censorship laws of our host nation.

Governments in countries in the Middle East control internet infrastructure and restrict connectivity by blocking encrypted services like WhatsApp, FaceTime, and Facebook Messenger. These governments also censor content that is anti-Islamic, critical of those governments, obscene, and offensive.

The region also faces political instability that could affect data center performance and reliability. Amazon Web Services recently announced that customer data stored in data centers in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates was unrecoverable after drone attacks by Iran in March and April.

>>> Families and Students Need Guidance on AI

In another scenario, a host nation may place tariffs on data transmitted back to the United States or use our data as a bargaining chip. In March, the World Trade Organization’s multilateral moratorium on customs duties for electronic transmissions lapsed. The United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement also prohibits tariffs on data transfers, but the future of this agreement is uncertain due to its ongoing review process and the recently renewed trade war between the United States and Canada.

Or say AI developers go to any of the European, South American, or East Asian countries that favor carbon emissions taxes or high fuel-use taxes. Like tariffs, taxes would be costs passed down to U.S. consumers.

These are some of the risks the United States faces if enough jurisdictions do not allow data center development domestically. Outside its boundaries, the United States loses control.

How AI Already Shapes Americans’ Daily Lives

Yet disillusionment with AI chatbots and disdain toward AI-generated content are growing. These objections are reasonable. People value human connection, critical thinking, and human multimedia rather than life-like imitations.

But rejection of AI is not as simple as abstaining from consumer-facing, general-purpose AI chatbots or objecting to AI-generated media. AI is embedded across systems in society, and regular people encounter uses of AI more than they realize.

For example, facial recognition technology or Face ID that allows users to unlock their phones, sign into password-protected accounts, and verify their age for age-restricted platforms with a quick scan of their face is enabled by AI software.

Prospective homeowners engage with home lending advisors who use AI-powered software to verify income and financial records and extract data from applications and other documents. AI can improve objectivity and efficiency of application reviews. Banks and credit-card companies use AI to analyze patterns and deviations in transactions for improved fraud detection.

Many physicians use AI to record and summarize clinical encounters. Modern medicine involves administrative tasks to maintain a medical history for patients, which helps inform patients and their providers. But these tasks are time-consuming and take away time providers can spend with patients. AI frees up some of providers’ time spent on administration.

Additionally, more physicians use the AI-powered medical search engine OpenEvidence to assist with complex diagnoses and research the latest treatment options. Modern medicine is advancing constantly; it is challenging even for specialists to remain informed of every new clinical trial, technique, or other development in their field. Unlike general-purpose AI tools, the platform complies with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) and is trained not on the open internet but on peer-reviewed medical literature, which helps ensure its output is accurate and relevant. The tool is only made available to health care professionals with verified credentials.

Drivers relying on GPS navigation obtain real-time traffic information, alerts, and faster routes due to AI. AI analyzes historical and live traffic conditions to estimate arrival times, predict slowdowns, and determine routes.

So whether or not you embrace AI, you likely unknowingly use it or you are on the receiving end of its use. And each of these examples involves processing and collecting sensitive data that should be safeguarded.

Why the United States Needs Data Centers at Home

U.S. AI data sovereignty means Americans’ data captured by AI systems is processed and stored in the United States. It also means it is governed and protected by U.S. laws and regulations and not subject to the whims of foreign governments. Maintaining data sovereignty requires sufficient data infrastructure.

>>> What’s Really Behind the Call to Regulate AI

This is why it matters that we build AI data centers in the United States. Wishing for AI’s extinction will not yield the desired results, and neither will widespread moratoriums on data center developments.

But in this current environment where data centers are politically unpopular, the future of data sovereignty is at stake.

Ratepayers are right to be concerned with how potential data center developments may affect their utility bills and access to necessary resources. Homeowners and buyers are right to be concerned with how it impacts homeownership and quality of life.

AI companies and data center developers must be honest, transparent, and fair—generous, even—to escape their villain trajectory. State and local leaders have an opportunity to respond to their constituents’ concerns and make favorable deals—ones that raise revenue for their jurisdictions and ensure that ratepayers are not suffering. Moratoriums on development and excessive demands stall, if not kill, negotiations.

If data center developers have nowhere to go domestically, they will have to go abroad. It could have similar consequences on the U.S. economy as offshoring in other industries, and it would be a shame after all the efforts to reshore manufacturing and other supply chains. Most certainly, it would relinquish data sovereignty.

This piece originally appeared in The National Interest
